principles.title: Need nothing, offer much
principles.motto: Arrive already full; then everything you give is a gift, not a plea.
principles.essence: Self-possession is the quiet fact that your life is already furnished: with work, friends, curiosity and pleasure. You do not come to another person to be filled; you come to share what overflows. Nothing is more restful to be near, or more quietly provoking.
principles.depth: Neediness is legible. People sense, within minutes, whether you approach them to give or to get, and a hunger for reassurance turns attraction into obligation. When David Buss surveyed mate preferences across 37 cultures (1989), emotional stability and maturity ranked near the top for both sexes, above looks and wealth. Attachment research points the same way: securely attached adults, as Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver described them (1987), can enjoy closeness without clutching at it, and their steadiness invites approach. Self-determination theory (Edward Deci and Richard Ryan) adds a subtler reason: when you act from autonomy rather than from a need for approval, your warmth reads as freely given, and only freely given warmth truly flatters. The philosophers knew it first. Epictetus opens his Enchiridion by dividing what is in our power from what is not; the self-possessed person has quietly placed another's desire in the second column and stopped trembling over it. Montaigne, in his essay on solitude, wrote that the greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself. The paradox is that the person who belongs to themselves is the one others most wish to be near: their attention is a choice, not a symptom.

tales.title: The Note of La Châtre
tales.who: Ninon de Lenclos, the Marquis de La Châtre, Queen Christina of Sweden
tales.source: Anecdotes recorded in 17th and 18th century French memoirs and letters, retold by Voltaire; the La Châtre story is a famous anecdote, not a documented scene
tales.tale:
The light is going gold in the rue des Tournelles, and the salon of Ninon de Lenclos is already half full. By the window sits a playwright the world will soon know as Molière. Two abbés, churchmen who have forgotten their prayer books, lean in. A young officer who came to look has stayed to listen. Ninon plays the lute a little. She talks a great deal. She laughs at exactly the right moment, which is rarer. She is past thirty, then past forty, and still the room does not empty.

There was beauty, yes, but what drew them was this: she wanted nothing from any of them. Her century offered a woman three safe roads, a husband, a convent, or a rich protector who could call her his, and she turned down all three. She lived on a small income and her wits. She chose her lovers the way she chose her books, for pleasure, and let them go without scenes. Her friends she kept for life.

The story the salons loved best is about the Marquis de La Châtre. Ordered off to the army, he could not bear to leave her free, and begged her for a signed promise that she would be faithful until he came home. Ninon, amused, wrote it out. As the story is told, some days later, in the arms of another man, she suddenly laughed and cried, "Ah, le bon billet qu'a La Châtre!" What a fine note La Châtre holds! The phrase passed into French as a saying for a promise worth nothing. The gossips drew a cruel lesson from it. The deeper one is kinder. A promise squeezed out by fear had never held her. Only her own choosing could.

In 1656 the strict church party at court persuaded the Queen Mother, Anne of Austria, to have Ninon shut away in a convent. Visitors came anyway. Among them was Christina, who had given up the throne of Sweden and found in this Frenchwoman without a title one of the freest minds in France. She is said to have spoken up for Ninon, and soon Ninon was free again.

She lived into her eighties. Near the end, a lawyer's son was brought to meet her, a clever, cheeky boy named François-Marie Arouet. In her will she left him two thousand francs to buy books. He became Voltaire. Even her last gift came with no strings. Go and read, she seemed to say. Go and become yourself.
tales.reveals: Ninon's magnetism came from a life that was already full of income, friendship, books and opinions of her own. Because she needed no one to complete her, being chosen by her was a compliment, and her company was a rest. The La Châtre note adds the corollary: fidelity begged for out of fear is only paper; the bond worth having is the one freely renewed.

tales.title: The Woman Socrates Brought His Friends to Hear
tales.who: Aspasia of Miletus and Pericles
tales.source: Plutarch, Life of Pericles 24 and 32; Plato, Menexenus; fragments of Athenian Old Comedy. Much of it is gossip or satire, and none of Aspasia's own words survive
tales.tale:
Evening in Athens. Oil lamps in a courtyard, cups of wine mixed with water, a ring of the most quarrelsome men in Greece. And at the center, unhurried, a woman from somewhere else, asking the question that made them doubt their last answer.

Her name was Aspasia. She had come from Miletus, an Ionian city across the Aegean Sea, around the middle of the fifth century BC, and Athens never quite decided what to make of her. Under the citizenship law of 451 BC, put forward by Pericles himself, a foreign woman could not be the lawful wife of a citizen. She had no Athenian family to lean on, no dowry, no standing. What she had was conversation.

That courtyard is only imagined. Plutarch, writing more than five hundred years later and sifting old gossip, says that Socrates sometimes came to her house with his friends, and that men even brought their wives to hear her, though her household was hardly thought respectable. In Plato's Menexenus, Socrates claims, perhaps with a wink, that Aspasia taught him the art of public speaking and wrote the famous funeral speech Pericles gave. Scholars still argue how much is a joke. But no one makes that joke about a woman with nothing to say.

Pericles was the most powerful man in Athens, a cool speaker they nicknamed the Olympian. After parting from his wife he lived with Aspasia openly. Plutarch keeps a detail his enemies found silly: every day, going out of the house and coming home again, Pericles kissed her. The comic poets called her a woman for hire, a Hera, the mistress of a tyrant, and blamed her for wars. When she was taken to court for disrespect to the gods, the story goes that Pericles, who never showed his feelings in public, wept before the jurors to save her. She was set free.

What stands out is how little Aspasia seems to have asked for. She did not chase the approval she could never have won. She made a room where the best minds wanted to be, and she let them come. Pericles did not give her worth. He was one of many who saw it.

When he died in the plague, she did not fade away. Plutarch reports she joined her life to Lysicles, a sheep dealer, who, the gossips sneered, soon became a leading man in Athens thanks to her. Not one word of her own survives. Only the door, and the men who kept walking through it.
tales.reveals: Aspasia had no status to trade on and no hope of the city's approval, so she stopped asking for it and made her own mind the prize. Self-possession is not a fortress; it is a well-lit room that people choose to enter. The most powerful man in Athens did not make her magnetic; he simply could not stay away.

practice: Before any date or meeting that matters this week, spend an hour on something that feeds you alone: a walk, a chapter, a craft. Arrive from your own life, not from waiting.
Notice one moment when you reach for reassurance (rereading a message, fishing for a compliment, checking whether she replied). Let it pass unasked, and observe that nothing collapses.
Offer one thing freely with no hook attached: a book, an introduction, a precise compliment. Then do not check whether it landed.
Say one clean no: decline an invitation you do not want, warmly and without a list of excuses.
principles.shadow: Self-possession curdles into coldness when needing nothing becomes a pose designed to make others chase you. If you are performing indifference to gain power, you are still needy, only in disguise; the real thing is warm and generous.

principles.title: The gift of total attention
principles.motto: Be wholly where you are, and she will want to be there too.
principles.essence: Most people are only half in the room, one eye on a phone, one ear on their own next sentence. Give a woman your full, unhurried attention and for that hour you become the most memorable person she has met. Presence is the rarest gift, and the most seductive.
principles.depth: Being attended to is one of the deepest human pleasures, because it is evidence that we exist for someone. Harry Reis and Phillip Shaver's intimacy process model (1988) places perceived responsiveness, the sense that another understands, values and cares about what we reveal, at the center of closeness, and decades of later research link it to attraction and lasting satisfaction. In a study of speed dates, Karen Huang and colleagues at Harvard (2017) found that people who asked more questions, especially follow-up questions, were liked more, and their partners were more willing to see them again. The follow-up is the tell: it proves you were listening rather than waiting for your turn. Attention is also bodily: steady eyes, an open posture, a pause before you answer. The philosophers were blunt about its worth. Simone Weil wrote to the poet Joë Bousquet in 1942 that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Martin Buber's I and Thou (1923) distinguishes treating someone as an It, an object to use or classify, from meeting them as a Thou, wholly and in the present. We feel that difference in our bones. Much of what we call charm is simply the skill of making another person feel like a Thou.

tales.title: Two Dinners in London
tales.who: Jennie Jerome (Lady Randolph Churchill), William Gladstone and Benjamin Disraeli
tales.when: late 1870s, as the story is told
tales.source: A celebrated anecdote attributed to Jennie Jerome in many later collections; no contemporary record confirms it, so read it as a parable rather than a transcript. Winston Churchill's line is from My Early Life (1930)
tales.tale:
Candlelight on silver, a long table, a young woman beside a famous man. The story that has followed Jennie Jerome for more than a century is a story about two dinners.

She was born in Brooklyn in 1854, the daughter of a daring Wall Street trader who loved racehorses and opera singers. At twenty she married Lord Randolph Churchill, having said yes three days after they met. London society took in the young American the way it took in every new thing: curious, and a little superior. She rode hard. She played the piano well enough to perform in public. She was dark-eyed and quick.

As it is usually told, Jennie was seated one evening beside William Ewart Gladstone, the great Liberal, the scholar of Homer, the man who would be Prime Minister four times. He was dazzling. He spoke of Ireland and the Church, of money and ancient books, and she followed as best she could, nodding, laughing in the right places. When the ladies left the table, she felt she had sat beside the cleverest man in England.

Some time later she found herself beside his great rival, Benjamin Disraeli: novelist, old dandy, Prime Minister, grey now and near the end of his life. And Disraeli did something else entirely. He asked her questions. He turned his whole famous face toward her and listened, and asked again, more closely, about her America, her opinions, her music. He caught her phrases and handed them back polished. He laughed at her jokes as if they had truly surprised him. When she rose from that table, the story goes, she felt that she was the cleverest woman in England.

Whether the dinners happened just so, no one can prove. It turns up in print only after both men were dead, in versions that do not agree. It lives on because everyone knows it. Most of us have met a Gladstone, brilliant and tiring, and come away feeling a little smaller. Far fewer have met a Disraeli.

He knew what he was doing. He was an old campaigner who had charmed a queen. But his way was not a trick. To make someone feel clever, you must notice where their mind is truly quick, and that takes real attention, which cannot be faked for long. Jennie learned the lesson. In later years politicians, soldiers and princes looked for her company, and her son Winston would write that she shone for him like the Evening Star.
tales.reveals: Brilliance makes people admire you; attention makes them want you near. Disraeli's power at that table came from turning the light away from himself and onto her, so that she met the best version of her own mind. People forget what you said, but they remember who they were beside you.

tales.title: The Stranger at the Sugar Merchants' Inn
tales.who: Jalal al-Din Rumi and Shams of Tabriz
tales.source: Hagiographies by Sipahsalar and Aflaki (14th century), Shams's own Maqalat (Discourses), and Rumi's poetry. The meeting stories are legends and differ widely
tales.tale:
Autumn in Konya. A learned man rides through the crowd, his students walking at his stirrup. A stranger in a black cloak steps into the road.

In 1244 Jalal al-Din of Konya was thirty-seven and already a man of standing: a scholar of religious law and a preacher like his father, respected by the Seljuk rulers. He was learned and admired, and, if his later poems tell the truth, asleep.

That November a wandering holy man, a dervish, came into Konya from Tabriz. He was perhaps sixty, wrapped in coarse black felt, and he called himself Shams, the Sun. He had slept in caravanserais, the inns of traveling traders, earned his bread by humble work, and moved on whenever people began to treat him as a saint. He had been searching, the stories say, for one companion who could bear his company.

The legends of their meeting are many, and they do not agree. In one of the best loved, Shams stepped into the path of Rumi's mount near the inn of the sugar merchants and caught the bridle. He asked a question that sounds simple and is not: who was greater, the Prophet Muhammad or the holy man Bayazid Bistami? For the Prophet had prayed, "We have not known You as You deserve to be known," while Bayazid had cried, "Glory be to me, how great is my majesty!" Rumi saw what the stranger was really asking. Whose thirst was greater, the one who is never filled, or the one filled by a single cup? He answered that the Prophet's thirst was endless, and in the answering, it is said, he came undone.

What came next is better known. The two men shut themselves away for weeks, some say months, talking, praying, sitting in silence. Rumi's teaching stopped. His students were shocked. The city whispered. What the watchers could not understand was a kind of attention neither man had ever found before. Shams wanted nothing of Rumi's learning or rank. He wanted Rumi, all of him, and gave himself the same way.

The jealousy of the students drove Shams away to Damascus, and Rumi's son brought him back. Then, around 1247, Shams vanished for good. Legend says he was murdered. No one knows. The sober scholar began to turn in the sama, the whirling prayer, and to pour out poetry, tens of thousands of lines, many signed with his friend's name. The great collection is still called the Divan of Shams of Tabriz.
tales.reveals: Rumi had the admiration of hundreds and it left him unmoved; it took one person's total, undistracted attention to wake him. Presence at this intensity is rare enough to feel like revelation. The deepest attraction is not to what someone has, but to how wholly they meet you.

practice: In your next important conversation, put your phone out of sight (not face down: out of sight) and leave it there until you part.
Ask at least three follow-up questions before you offer a story of your own. Let each question prove you heard the answer to the last.
Practise the half-second pause: before you reply, let what she said land. It tells her that her words have weight.
Afterward, write down one specific thing she said that surprised you. If you cannot, you were not fully there.
principles.shadow: Attention used as a technique, switched on to conquer and off once you have won, is counterfeit, and people feel the drop like a door closing. Never feign fascination to extract something; give attention because the person deserves it, or not at all.

principles.title: Sprezzatura: the art of effortless grace
principles.motto: Work hard in private; in company, let everything look like play.
principles.essence: Grace is the visible absence of strain. The people we find most attractive seem to move through a room, a conversation or a small crisis without grasping, as if what they do costs them nothing. That ease is almost always the fruit of hidden practice, and of a mind not busy watching itself.
principles.depth: Baldassare Castiglione gave this quality its name: sprezzatura, a studied nonchalance that hides the labor behind it. Why does it work? Psychologists speak of processing fluency: what is easy to perceive feels pleasant, familiar and right, and Rolf Reber, Norbert Schwarz and Piotr Winkielman (2004) argued that fluency is part of why things strike us as beautiful. An effortless manner is fluent to watch; visible strain makes the observer strain too. There is also self-monitoring. Under pressure, attention turns inward and skilled performance falls apart, the choking that Sian Beilock and others have studied. Ease signals someone not anxious about the outcome, and that security is itself attractive. Effortless does not mean flawless. Elliot Aronson and colleagues (1966) found that a highly competent person who clumsily spilled coffee was rated more likable than one who did not, though later work showed this pratfall effect depends heavily on the observer and the situation. A small, unflustered imperfection humanizes. The Taoist classic Zhuangzi tells of Cook Ding, whose blade never dulled because after years of practice he cut along the natural joints of the ox without forcing: skill so complete it looks like rest. That is the ideal: not laziness, but mastery relaxed enough to play.

tales.title: Four Evenings at Urbino
tales.who: Baldassare Castiglione, Duchess Elisabetta Gonzaga, Emilia Pia, Count Ludovico da Canossa, Pietro Bembo
tales.source: Baldassare Castiglione, Il libro del Cortegiano (The Book of the Courtier, 1528), Books I and IV; real people in a literary recreation of their conversations
tales.tale:
Night on a hill in the Marche. The Duke has gone to bed, but in the Duchess's rooms the candles still burn, and someone is laughing.

In the spring of 1507 the palace of Urbino may have been the finest house in Italy. Duke Guidobaldo da Montefeltro, crippled by gout, kept early hours. His wife, Elisabetta Gonzaga, did not. After supper the court gathered around her: soldiers, poets, a future cardinal, a few ladies who could out-talk them all, and the Duchess's companion Emilia Pia, who kept order with a raised eyebrow.

Years later one of those courtiers, Baldassare Castiglione, set down what he remembered, or what he wished had been said, as The Book of the Courtier. One evening, he wrote, the company chose a game: they would describe in words the perfect courtier, the ideal servant of a prince. Count Ludovico da Canossa was given the task, and the others heckled him.

Must the courtier be nobly born? A soldier first? Should he dance, sing, draw? Ludovico answered patiently, and then, almost in passing, gave them the idea that would outlive them all. Whatever the courtier does, he said, should be done with a certain sprezzatura, a graceful carelessness that hides the art behind it and makes everything he does seem to cost no effort. A hard thing done easily makes us marvel. Straining that shows will spoil even real skill. He mocked the dancer counting his steps with a frown, the rider stiff as a statue, the man who drops learned words into every sentence to be noticed.

The ladies teased him for teaching gentlemen to deceive. The count gave way so good-humoredly that he showed them, without trying, the very thing he meant.

The talk ran on for four nights. On the last, the poet Pietro Bembo was carried away by a speech on love, rising from the body to the soul, and from the soul to the beauty of God, until Emilia Pia took the hem of his robe and gave it a little shake to bring him back to earth. Someone opened the windows. The night had gone unnoticed. Over the peak of Monte Catria the dawn was coming up rose-colored, and the birds were already singing.

When the book was printed in 1528, the Duke and Duchess were dead and the bright days of Urbino were over. But the word lived on: a name for grace that hides its labor so well it looks like a gift.
tales.reveals: Castiglione saw that what charms us is not skill alone but skill worn lightly. At Urbino ease was a shared art: wit, teasing and deep talk all looked spontaneous because everyone had been preparing for a lifetime. Sprezzatura is also a courtesy, because it spares others the sight of your effort.

tales.title: The Stilt-Walker from Bristol
tales.who: Archibald Leach, who became Cary Grant
tales.source: Biographies of Cary Grant and his own memoir series 'Archie Leach' (Ladies' Home Journal, 1963); the famous quotes are widely attributed rather than securely documented
tales.tale:
A boy on stilts, high above the crowd, grinning as if it were the easiest thing in the world. No one watching could count the falls behind it.

His name was Archibald Alexander Leach, and he was born in Bristol in 1904, in a house that was cold in every sense. His father pressed suits in a clothing factory and drank. His mother, Elsie, was anxious and watchful. When Archie was about nine he came home from school and she was gone. He was told she had gone to the seaside to rest. In truth she was shut away in a hospital for the mentally ill, and he did not learn she was alive until he was in his thirties.

At fourteen the boy found a family of another kind: Bob Pender's troupe of acrobats and comic stilt-walkers. He learned to tumble, to fall without getting hurt, to time a comic fall so exactly that the audience never saw the counting behind it. In 1920 the troupe sailed for New York, and when it went home he stayed. He walked on stilts at Coney Island, played in vaudeville, the variety stage, and watched how rich men in Manhattan restaurants held a cigarette and wore a coat.

He took a voice that was half Bristol music hall and blended it into something no one could place, an accent from nowhere. He watched how the English song-and-dance man Jack Buchanan moved. When Paramount signed him in 1931, the studio asked for a new name, and Archie Leach became Cary Grant: tanned, tailored, amused.

Audiences saw the opposite of effort. In Bringing Up Baby (1938) and His Girl Friday (1940) he took falls, did double takes, fired off lines at machine-gun speed, all the while seeming to enjoy a private joke. The acrobat's training was hidden because it was complete. He never looked as though he were trying to charm. That is exactly why he did.

The price was paid off camera. He married five times and later spoke frankly about the fear beneath the polish. He is often quoted as saying that he pretended to be somebody he wanted to be until finally he became that person, or that person became him. And when someone told him that everyone wanted to be Cary Grant, he is said to have answered: so do I.

Ease, then, can be built. It is learned the way a tumbler learns to fall: thousands of times, until the body forgets to be afraid.
tales.reveals: Cary Grant's effortlessness was the most worked-on thing about him, built from an acrobat's discipline and years of close watching. His story shows that ease is not the birthright of the confident; it can be practised into being, until mask and face grow together. It also shows the cost of hiding all strain: the person inside still needs somewhere to be unguarded.

practice: Choose one thing you do in company (a particular story, a cocktail, a basic dance step) and rehearse it privately until you could do it while thinking about something else.
Slow down by a quarter: walk, speak and reach for things a little more slowly than feels natural. Hurry reads as anxiety.
When you make a small mistake in front of someone this week, name it lightly and move on. Laughing at yourself is the fastest proof of ease.
Stop announcing your effort: do not mention how long it took or how hard it was. Let the thing speak.
principles.shadow: Sprezzatura turns sour when it becomes contempt for effort itself, or a mask so complete that no one is ever allowed to see you try, fail or care. Ease should put others at ease; if it makes them feel clumsy or shut out, you have mistaken nonchalance for superiority.

principles.title: Leave something unsaid
principles.motto: Show the light in the window, never the whole house.
principles.essence: Desire is curiosity with a body. When everything about you is visible at once there is nothing left to wonder about; when something stays in shadow, the other person's imagination goes to work on your behalf. Reveal yourself truthfully, but not all at once.
principles.depth: George Loewenstein's information-gap theory (1994) holds that curiosity spikes when we know enough to sense a gap but not enough to close it. Total opacity bores, total exposure bores too, and the pull lives in between. A provocative study by Michael Norton, Jeana Frost and Dan Ariely (2007), titled Less Is More, found that people tended to like strangers less as they learned more of their traits, because each new fact raised the chance of finding a dissimilarity. The finding was challenged: Harry Reis and colleagues (2011) showed that in live interaction, getting to know someone usually increased liking. Together the two results are instructive: mystery is a matter of pacing, not concealment. Disclosure that unfolds gradually builds intimacy, while disclosure dumped all at once forecloses it. The Zeigarnik effect, Bluma Zeigarnik's 1927 claim that unfinished tasks linger in memory, has replicated less reliably than its fame suggests, but the intuition behind it is old. Ernest Hemingway wrote in Death in the Afternoon (1932) that the dignity of an iceberg's movement comes from only an eighth of it showing above water. Junichiro Tanizaki's essay In Praise of Shadows (1933) argued that beauty lives in half-light. A person, too, is lovelier lit from the side.

tales.title: The Woman Who Walked Away
tales.who: Greta Garbo
tales.source: Film records and biographies of Garbo; the line 'I want to be alone' is from Grand Hotel (1932), and her later correction is reported by biographers
tales.tale:
A woman in dark glasses and a slouch hat turns into a shop doorway, and when the photographer reaches the corner, she is gone. She did this for almost fifty years.

In 1941 Greta Garbo was thirty-six, perhaps the most famous face in the world, and the star of a comedy, Two-Faced Woman, that the critics disliked. MGM planned more pictures. The war had closed the European markets that loved her best. She told friends she would wait. She waited for the rest of her life.

She had come to Hollywood in 1925, a shy Swedish girl who had once modeled hats for a Stockholm department store. Within a few years she was the great puzzle of the screen. Her art was holding back: a face that seemed to be thinking something it would not say. For the last shot of Queen Christina (1933), the director Rouben Mamoulian told her to make her mind a blank as the camera held on her at the front of a ship. Audiences filled that empty face with every grief they had ever known.

Off screen she did the same. She gave almost no interviews, skipped premieres, stayed away from the parties where everyone else went to be seen. In Grand Hotel her character says, "I want to be alone," and the line became her legend. Biographers report that she later protested she had never said it about herself. What she had said was that she wanted to be let alone. There is a world of difference between the two.

After 1941 she settled in New York, in an apartment on East 52nd Street filled with paintings, and she walked. In trousers and flat shoes she covered miles of Manhattan almost every day. Photographers hunted her. Strangers whispered on the pavement. Every few years a rumor of a comeback rose, and fell.

Her silence did what no studio's publicity men could have done. Because she never explained herself, never grew old on screen, never fed the gossip columns, she stayed what she had been in the dark of the cinema: a question. When she died in 1990, at eighty-four, she was more of a mystery than when she left.

Garbo was not playing a game. By every account she was truly private, sometimes painfully so. But her life shows that what is held back keeps its power to fascinate. Give the imagination room, and it will write a better story than any confession.
tales.reveals: Garbo's power on screen and off came from what she withheld: a face that did not explain itself, a life that refused to perform. Mystery is not a lie; it is declining to narrate everything, which leaves others room to wonder. It works best when, as with her, the reserve is real.

tales.title: Behind the Blinds of Heian-kyo
tales.who: Sei Shonagon, Murasaki Shikibu and the courtiers of Heian Japan
tales.source: Sei Shonagon, The Pillow Book (c. 1002); Murasaki Shikibu, The Tale of Genji (c. 1008, a work of fiction) and her diary
tales.tale:
A bamboo blind at the edge of a veranda. Behind it, a curtain of silk. Behind that, a woman no visitor will see clearly.

Around the year 1000, in the capital called Heian-kyo, a nobleman could fall in love with a woman he had never properly seen. Ladies of the court lived behind such layers, the silk curtains hung on movable lacquered stands. Even a visitor allowed to speak with her usually spoke through a screen. She stayed a voice, a scent, a shadow.

So courtship ran on hints. At a festival procession a man might glimpse the edge of a sleeve spilling from the blinds of an ox carriage: many layers of silk in shaded colors, chosen with fierce care to suit the season. From that hem he would guess at her taste, and from her taste, her heart. Or he might peer through a gap in a brushwood fence, as Prince Genji does in Murasaki Shikibu's novel, a work of fiction, when he first glimpses the girl who will become the great love of his life.

Then came the poem. He wrote thirty-one syllables on paper whose color, weight and fold all carried meaning, perhaps tied to a spray of blossom, and sent it by messenger. Everything was judged: the brushwork, the quiet nods to older poems, the restraint. A reply might come quickly, or slowly, or in another woman's hand, which was a polite refusal. If the letters went well, he might at last be let in at night, behind the curtains, in the dark.

Even then the mystery was not used up. Custom said he must leave before dawn and send a morning-after poem, and Sei Shonagon, lady-in-waiting to the Empress Teishi, had firm views on the matter. In The Pillow Book she sketches the ideal lover rising unwillingly in the half-dark, sighing, lingering, murmuring at the door about how long the day will be until night comes again. She is merciless about the other kind, who jumps up briskly, rummages noisily for his fan and his sash, and bustles off as if he had business elsewhere.

Desire feeds on what is half seen. A woman known by her handwriting and her colors, a man known by a voice through a screen and a poem left at dawn: each had to be imagined, and to imagine is to long. Even lovers who had shared a night parted while it was still dark, so that each would remember the other half seen.
tales.reveals: Heian courtship made partial knowledge into an art: a sleeve, a scent or a line of handwriting stood for a whole person and invited the other to dream. Mystery here is not coldness but pacing, the self revealed in fragments that are each exquisite. What is glimpsed is wanted more than what is displayed.

practice: In your next getting-to-know-you conversation, give one answer that is true but partial, and promise the rest another time. Then keep that promise.
Keep one part of your life offline this month: a project, a place or a pleasure you never post about. Let it be discovered in person.
End a good evening or call at its high point, not after it has wound down.
Once this week, write instead of texting: a short handwritten note on paper you chose, with no explanation of why.
principles.shadow: Mystery becomes manipulation when it means hiding what she has a right to know (a partner, an intention, a fact that would change her choice) or going silent to make her anxious. Hold back the story, never the truth.

principles.title: Arrive as a story
principles.motto: People fall for the story before they fall for the person.
principles.essence: Before a woman knows you, she knows what is said about you and how you first appear. Shape your entrance and your reputation with intention, so that meeting you feels like stepping into a tale. Then be someone who lives up to it.
principles.depth: We understand one another through stories long before we understand facts. Melanie Green and Timothy Brock (2000) showed that when people are transported into a narrative, absorbed in its images and feelings, they adopt more of its beliefs and argue against it less. A person who arrives wrapped in a story invites that same absorption. The halo effect, named by Edward Thorndike in 1920 and demonstrated experimentally by Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson (1977), shows how one vivid impression colors everything we judge afterward. First impressions form astonishingly fast: Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov (2006) found that people judged traits such as trustworthiness from a face shown for a tenth of a second, and that longer looks mostly made them more confident rather than different. Philosophy has long held that persons are partly made of narrative. Paul Ricoeur called it narrative identity, the self as the story one tells and is told; Roland Barthes, in Mythologies (1957), dissected how images harden into myths that seem simply natural. None of this means inventing a false self. It means choosing which true things to dramatize, giving your life the shape of a tale, and remembering that setting, timing and the first glimpse are part of what you say.

tales.title: Aphrodite on the Cydnus
tales.who: Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony
tales.source: Plutarch, Life of Antony 25 to 27 (written c. AD 100, drawing on earlier accounts); later reworked by Shakespeare in Antony and Cleopatra
tales.tale:
Purple sails on a river. Silver oars keeping time to flutes. And on the banks of the Cydnus, a whole city running to the water.

In 41 BC Mark Antony, master of the Roman East after the victory at Philippi, was holding court at Tarsus in Cilicia. He was summoning the kings and queens whose thrones now hung on his word. One of his letters went to Alexandria. The Queen of Egypt was to come and answer charges that she had helped the cause of Caesar's murderers.

Cleopatra was twenty-eight. She had been Julius Caesar's lover and had borne him a son. She spoke many languages, ruled the richest kingdom in the Mediterranean, and knew exactly how the summons looked. A queen who came as the accused would be judged as one. So she ignored the letters that followed the first, took her time, and came as something else entirely.

Plutarch, writing well over a century later, tells the scene as it had come down to him. She sailed up the river in a barge with a gilded stern, purple sails spread, silver oars keeping time to the music of flutes, pipes and lyres. She lay beneath a canopy sprinkled with gold, dressed like Aphrodite in a painting, while boys dressed as Cupids stood on either side fanning her. Her loveliest maids, dressed as sea nymphs and Graces, held the rudders and the ropes. Rich perfumes drifted from the boat to the riverbanks.

People ran along the shore after her, and the city emptied until, Plutarch says, Antony was left sitting alone on his judge's seat in the marketplace. And a rumor spread through Tarsus that Aphrodite had come to revel with Dionysus for the good of Asia. Antony liked to show himself in the East as the new Dionysus, god of wine. Cleopatra had simply written herself into his own myth, as its goddess.

He sent an invitation to dinner. She replied that he should come to her instead. He went and found a feast lit by more lamps than he had ever seen, hung and set out in clever patterns. The next evening he tried to outdo her and failed, and was the first to joke about his own plain table. She caught his tone at once, Plutarch notes, and answered in kind, boldly, with the blunt humor of a soldier.

The meeting had been set up as a trial. By the time it was over, the judge was following the accused home to Alexandria.
tales.reveals: Cleopatra turned a summons into a spectacle, and a hearing into a love story, by choosing the frame before anyone else could. She did not argue her case; she arrived as a myth that matched her audience's own. Notice too that the myth only opened the door: what held Antony was her wit at table.

tales.title: The Morning After Childe Harold
tales.who: George Gordon, Lord Byron
tales.source: Thomas Moore, Letters and Journals of Lord Byron, with Notices of His Life (1830), which records Byron's famous remark; publication details from John Murray's records and Byron's letters
tales.tale:
A young lord limps up St James's Street in the grey London winter, carrying debts, a bad reputation and a long poem. In a few weeks every door in the city will open to him.

In February 1812, George Gordon, sixth Lord Byron, was twenty-four. He was back from two years of wandering through Portugal, Spain, Albania and Greece, and was little known beyond a few clubs. He had a crumbling abbey in Nottinghamshire, a lame foot he hid as best he could, a satire that had made him enemies, and a manuscript: a long poem, written in the old verse form of Spenser, about a weary young nobleman who turns his back on pleasure to wander among the ruins of Europe.

On 27 February he made his first speech in the House of Lords, defending the Nottinghamshire frame-breakers, workers who faced the gallows for smashing the new machines. It was eloquent, and almost no one listened. Then, on 10 March, John Murray published the first two cantos, or parts, of Childe Harold's Pilgrimage. The first edition, five hundred costly copies in a large format, sold out in three days.

Overnight, London decided that the poet was the poem. Here was Harold himself: brooding, beautiful, noble, with some nameless sin behind him and the dust of Greece on his boots. Invitations piled up at his rooms in St James's Street. Hostesses fought for him. Women wrote to him without signing their names. Lady Caroline Lamb, before she had even met him, wrote in her journal that he was mad, bad and dangerous to know, which only made her more eager to know him.

Byron understood what had happened and played to it. He kept himself pale and slender, it was said, on biscuits, soda water and vinegar. He sat for a portrait in Albanian dress. He let rumors of dark adventures swell unanswered. Years later his friend Thomas Moore recorded the words Byron used for that spring: he awoke one morning and found himself famous.

The legend carried him into more drawing rooms, more beds and more trouble than any poem could. It also became a cage. Within four years debt and scandal drove him out of England for good, and the man who had so enjoyed being a story found he could no longer change its ending. He died at Missolonghi in 1824, at thirty-six, helping the Greeks fight for their freedom, in the land that had first given him his myth.
tales.reveals: Byron arrived not as a man but as a character, and London fell for the character first. His story shows how powerfully a single vivid narrative can precede and magnify a person. It also warns that a myth you do not steer will, in the end, steer you.

practice: Choose one true, vivid story about yourself (a place you lived, a thing you made, a risk you took) and offer it, briefly, where you would normally give your job title.
Design one entrance this week: arrive once the gathering has warmed up, wear one memorable detail, and greet the host before anyone else.
Invite someone into a setting that tells a story: not the usual bar, but a rooftop, a night market, a museum's late opening.
Let others carry your myth. Do not tell your best stories about yourself; let a friend tell them for you.
principles.shadow: A myth built on lies is fraud, and a persona you cannot live up to will collapse in intimacy and wound whoever believed it. Dramatize what is true, never fabricate a self to win a woman, and set the costume down once she wants to know the person.

principles.title: Intensity shared becomes attraction
principles.motto: Meet on the swaying bridge, and let the racing heart find you.
principles.essence: A pounding heart does not always know why it pounds. When you share intensity with a woman, a climb, a storm, a dance, a risk, her body searches for a cause and often settles on you. Seek out moments that quicken the pulse, and be the steady, warm face in the middle of them.
principles.depth: In 1962 Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer proposed a two-factor theory of emotion: the body supplies raw arousal, and the mind reads the situation to decide what that arousal means. A racing pulse beside an attractive stranger can be read as desire, a process psychologists call misattribution of arousal. The idea has been tested and argued over for half a century. Douglas Kenrick and Robert Cialdini (1977) suggested the effect might come from relief rather than confusion; a meta-analysis by Craig Foster and colleagues (1998) concluded that it is real but modest. White, Fishbein and Rutstein (1981) found something subtler: arousal amplifies whatever is already there, so it raised attraction to an appealing partner and lowered it to an unappealing one. Arousal does not create a spark; it fans one. Arthur Aron's team (2000) showed the same for couples: partners who did a novel, physically exciting task together reported more satisfaction afterwards than those who did something dull. The poets knew it first. Sappho, in fragment 31, describes love as an alarm in the body: the tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under the skin, the ears hum. Plato's Phaedrus calls it a divine madness. Shared intensity gives that madness somewhere to land.

tales.title: The Woman on the Swaying Bridge
tales.who: Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, and the men of the Capilano Canyon
tales.where: Capilano Canyon, North Vancouver, British Columbia
tales.source: Dutton and Aron, 'Some evidence for heightened sexual attraction under conditions of high anxiety', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1974
tales.tale:
Wind moves through the canyon, and the bridge moves with it. The Capilano Suspension Bridge is a walkway of boards hung on wire cables, about five feet wide and four hundred and fifty feet long, and it hangs some two hundred and thirty feet above rocks and shallow rapids. The handrails are low. It tilts. It wobbles. Somewhere near the middle, every walker feels that the next step might tip them over the side.

In the early 1970s two psychologists from the University of British Columbia, Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, sent a young woman out onto that bridge. She waited for men crossing alone and stopped them in the middle, high above the water. Would they help with a class project, she asked, on the effects of scenic attractions on creativity? Each man filled in a short questionnaire. Then he wrote a brief story about a picture: a young woman covering her face with one hand and reaching out with the other. When he was done, she tore a corner off the page, wrote her name and telephone number on it, and said that if he wanted to hear more about the study, he could call her.

Upriver stood a second bridge, a solid cedar span only ten feet above a gentle stream. The same woman ran the same routine there. Same smile. Same scrap of paper.

The difference was plain. Of the men who took her number on the swaying bridge, nine out of eighteen telephoned. On the solid bridge, two out of sixteen did. The stories the frightened men wrote were also richer in sexual imagery. And when the researchers sent a man out to ask the questions instead, the bridges made no difference at all.

Dutton and Aron read it this way. A man in the middle of a frightening bridge has a hammering heart, damp palms, quick breath. Suddenly a lovely stranger stands before him, smiling. His body is already shouting, and his mind, looking for a reason, finds her. The researchers backed the field study with laboratory work, yet their reading has been debated ever since. Some argue that what the men felt was relief, and that she was simply part of the relief.

Either way, the river kept running far below. A phone number on a scrap of paper meant more when it was handed over high above the rocks, with the boards still swaying underfoot.
tales.reveals: The body does not file its sensations neatly; it borrows the nearest explanation. Meet someone where the pulse is already high, and you become part of what the pulse means. But note the control: the effect needed a woman they already found appealing. Intensity amplifies attraction; it cannot invent it.

tales.title: The Admiral Comes Back from the Nile
tales.who: Horatio Nelson and Emma Hamilton
tales.where: Naples, and the voyage to Palermo
tales.source: Nelson's letter to his wife Fanny, 25 September 1798; accounts in the Hamilton and Nelson papers and the biographies of Tom Pocock and Kate Williams
tales.tale:
The Bay of Naples was crowded with boats, and every boat was turned toward one ship. On 22 September 1798 the Vanguard, a battered ship of the line, came slowly into the bay. On board stood Rear Admiral Horatio Nelson, forty years old. He had lost his right arm in a battle at Tenerife the year before. He was still dizzy from a head wound taken at the mouth of the Nile seven weeks earlier. There, off Aboukir Bay, his fleet had destroyed Napoleon's. All Naples was on the water to greet him.

In one of the boats sat the British ambassador, Sir William Hamilton, and his wife Emma, thirty three. She was famous across Europe for her beauty and for her 'Attitudes', silent performances in which, with only a shawl and her body, she became Medea or a weeping Niobe. Nelson told his wife what happened next, in a letter. The scene in the boat was terribly affecting, he wrote. Emma flew up, cried out 'O God, is it possible?', and fell into his arm more dead than alive.

She took him to the Palazzo Sessa and nursed him. A week later, for his fortieth birthday, she threw a ball for some seventeen hundred guests. Candles, music, and a hero at the center of it all.

Then the light turned. The French were marching on Naples, and in December the royal family had to flee. Emma helped arrange the secret transfer of the royal jewels and treasure to Nelson's ship. On the crossing to Palermo the Vanguard ran into one of the worst storms Nelson said he had ever known. Sails tore. The queen's servants prayed aloud. Emma, who did not get seasick, moved from bed to bed in the rolling dark, comforting the royal children. The youngest prince, six years old, died of convulsions in her arms on Christmas Day.

Think of all they had carried together in three months: fear, glory, nursing, grief. A wounded hero, and a performer who had found her finest role in a crisis. Their love affair seems to have begun in Palermo in 1799. Their daughter Horatia was born in 1801. Nelson left his wife Fanny.

London society never forgave either of them. But by then the storm had already done its work.
tales.reveals: Nelson and Emma met in an atmosphere of fever: victory, wounds, flight and death. Such intensity binds two people quickly and deeply. It also bound two married people who might, in calmer weather, have stayed friends, and the cost was paid by Fanny and in the end by Emma, who died in poverty in Calais in 1815.

practice: Plan one date this week that raises the pulse: a steep walk to a viewpoint, a dance class, a fast ride at a fair, a cold swim. Stay close and calm inside the excitement.
When something thrilling happens to you both, say so aloud ('My heart is going like a drum') so the feeling becomes shared rather than private.
With a long-time partner, swap one familiar evening for something neither of you has done before; novelty and mild challenge renew the charge.
After the intensity peaks, give a quiet moment: a hand on the arm, a drink together. The descent is where the bond settles.
principles.shadow: Manufacturing danger, fear or crisis to make someone attach to you is manipulation, and the bond it builds is unstable. Intensity should be an adventure you both choose, never a storm you create for the other person to survive.

principles.title: Break the script
principles.motto: The expected is forgiven; the unexpected is remembered.
principles.essence: Attraction wakes when the script breaks. Everyone arrives through the door they were expected to use; arrive through another, with a gesture no one predicted, and you are suddenly seen in sharp focus. Surprise is not chaos: it is a small, well-judged departure that reveals who you are.
principles.depth: The brain is a prediction machine, and it rewards the unpredicted. In work summarised by Wolfram Schultz, Peter Dayan and Read Montague (Science, 1997), dopamine neurons in monkeys fired strongly at an unexpected reward and barely at all once the same reward became predictable: the signal tracks the gap between what was expected and what arrived. Gregory Berns and colleagues (2001) found that human reward areas responded more to squirts of juice and water delivered in an unpredictable sequence than in a predictable one. Daniel Berlyne, in Conflict, Arousal and Curiosity (1960), listed novelty and surprise among the 'collative' qualities that draw attention and interest. So the person who departs from the script is not just noticed; they are, in a literal sense, rewarding. Philosophy reached the same point by other roads. Aristotle in the Poetics prized the reversal, events that happen contrary to expectation yet follow from one another, because surprise that makes sense afterwards moves us most. Kierkegaard, in the essay 'Rotation of Crops' in Either/Or (1843), warned that boredom is the root of much evil and that the cure is not endless change of scene but changing how one cultivates the same field. The best surprise is not random. It is unexpected, then obviously right.

tales.title: The Bedroll at the Palace Gate
tales.who: Cleopatra VII and Julius Caesar
tales.source: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 49; a different version in Cassius Dio, Roman History 42.34
tales.tale:
Night was falling on Alexandria, and a small boat slid along the shore toward the palace. It was the autumn of 48 BC. Inside the palace, Julius Caesar was living as an uninvited guest. He had come chasing his rival Pompey, only to be handed Pompey's severed head by the advisers of the boy king Ptolemy XIII. Egypt was at war with itself. Ptolemy's sister and co-ruler, Cleopatra, twenty one years old, had been driven from the capital and was camped beyond the eastern desert with a small army. Between her and the palace stood her brother's troops, his guards, and a city full of people who would gladly see her dead.

Caesar had called both of them to settle their quarrel before him. Ptolemy could simply walk in. Cleopatra could not.

So she did not walk. Plutarch tells how she took one trusted friend, Apollodorus the Sicilian, and a small boat, and came along the shore as darkness fell. There was no way past the gates unseen. So she lay down at full length inside a bed sack, the kind used to bundle up bedding and rugs. Apollodorus tied it shut with a strap, lifted it to his shoulder, and carried it through the doors, past the guards, into the rooms of the most powerful man in the Mediterranean. (The famous carpet was added by later storytellers; Plutarch's word means a sack for bedding.)

Picture the moment as Caesar knew it. A servant comes in with a bundle. The strap is loosened. Out of the cloth rises the queen of Egypt, her hair a little out of place, her manner entirely calm, ready to argue her case in fluent Greek. Plutarch says it was this trick that first won Caesar over, because it showed her boldness, and that her company and charm then did the rest. Within days Caesar ordered the brother and sister to make peace on terms that favoured her. Within months they were lovers, and she would bear him a son.

Cassius Dio, writing later, tells it another way. In his telling she sent to ask for a meeting, then came dressed to show her majesty and her sorrow at once.

Either way, Cleopatra understood the same thing. Someone waiting in the outer room is one more voice asking for favours. A woman who arrives where no one could have guessed is a story.
tales.reveals: Cleopatra did not merely surprise Caesar; the surprise was an argument. It proved, in a single gesture, her nerve, her wit and her willingness to stake everything. The most powerful surprises tell the other person who you are faster than any speech.

tales.title: The Cloak in the Mud
tales.who: Walter Raleigh and Elizabeth I
tales.source: Thomas Fuller, The History of the Worthies of England (1662); widely regarded by historians as legend
tales.tale:
Picture a path, a patch of mud, and a queen who has stopped at the edge of it. The story is almost certainly a legend, and it is a good one. It was first written down by the clergyman Thomas Fuller in 1662, some eighty years after it is supposed to have happened, in his chatty and fond History of the Worthies of England.

Walter Raleigh, Fuller says, was a young captain lately back from the wars in Ireland. He came to court well dressed, and Fuller adds a detail that makes the whole tale glow: his clothes were then a considerable part of his estate. He had no great family behind him, no title, no fortune. What he had was a new plush cloak and a quick eye.

One day he found the Queen out walking, and she came to a muddy place in the path. Elizabeth paused. Behind her stood courtiers who had waited years for one moment of her notice, men who knew every rule of how to approach her. Not one of them had a rule for a puddle.

Raleigh did not wait for a rule. He swept off his cloak, the most valuable thing he owned, and spread it over the mud. The Queen, Fuller writes, trod gently over it, and afterwards rewarded him with many suits for so free and seasonable a tender of so fair a footcloth. In plain words: a fine gift, at the right time.

Fuller tells a second story about Raleigh in the same breath. The young man, it is said, scratched a line on a window pane with a diamond: 'Fain would I climb, yet fear I to fall.' The Queen, finding it, wrote beneath: 'If thy heart fails thee, climb not at all.'

Whatever the truth of either tale, the rise was real. Within a few years Raleigh was a royal favourite, knighted in 1585, granted estates and monopolies (the sole right to trade in certain goods), made Captain of the Queen's Guard. The danger of being a favourite was real too. When Elizabeth found out in 1592 that he had secretly married one of her maids of honour, Bess Throckmorton, she sent them both to the Tower.

People told the cloak story again and again because it holds something true. In a court where everyone played the same careful game, one man broke the script with a gesture that was quick, generous, a little foolish, and perfectly timed. Mud, a cloak, a queen's light step.
tales.reveals: The surprise worked because it cost him something and was offered without calculation (or with calculation so quick it looked like instinct). A gesture outside the script, made at the right second and at a real price, says more than years of correct behaviour.

practice: Notice the script of your next date or evening together (same place, same time, same talk) and change one element: a different door, a picnic instead of a restaurant, a question nobody asks.
Prepare one small, specific surprise rooted in something she mentioned weeks ago: the book she wanted, the dish from her childhood. The memory makes the surprise land.
Let yourself be unexpected in conversation: disagree warmly, reveal an unlikely passion, answer a routine question with a real one.
Keep the rhythm unpredictable but the character steady: surprise in what you do, reliability in who you are.
principles.shadow: Surprise turns to manipulation when it is used to destabilise: hot and cold for its own sake, ambushes, gestures that leave the other person no room to say no. Never surprise her with what she has not consented to; the best surprises are gifts that can be refused.

principles.title: Tease, spar, delight
principles.motto: Spar as equals, laugh as accomplices, and let the game grow warm.
principles.essence: Play is how two people test each other without wounding. Teasing, sparring, private jokes and invented games all say: I believe you are strong enough to be played with, and I am free enough to play. Keep it light and keep it mutual, and you build a small world only the two of you live in.
principles.depth: Johan Huizinga, in Homo Ludens (1938), argued that play is older than culture: a free activity, set apart from ordinary life, with its own rules and its own enclosed space, a 'magic circle' as later writers called it. Lovers who play together build exactly such a circle. Friedrich Schiller went further in his Letters on the Aesthetic Education of Man (1795): a person is only fully human when he plays. Science has followed. Jaak Panksepp traced a dedicated PLAY system in the mammalian brain and showed that young rats emit ultrasonic chirps, something like laughter, when tickled (Panksepp and Burgdorf, 2003). In adults, Garry Chick and colleagues (2012) found that playfulness ranked among the traits both men and women most wanted in a long-term partner, and suggested it signals good humour, low aggression and youthful vitality. Dacher Keltner's team, in their 1998 study of teasing and their 2001 review 'Just teasing', described teasing as a provocation softened by signals of play: the raised eyebrow, the exaggerated tone, the grin. Done well, among friends and lovers, it builds closeness; done badly, it hurts. The art is in those signals. Play is also a test of equality: you only spar with someone you think can hit back.

tales.title: Fire at Cirey
tales.who: Voltaire and Emilie du Chatelet
tales.source: The letters of Voltaire and of Emilie du Chatelet; Madame de Graffigny's letters from Cirey (1738 to 1739); the Academie des sciences prize essays on fire (published 1739)
tales.tale:
Candles burning past midnight, and two voices arguing, laughing, arguing again. In 1734 Voltaire was in trouble again. His Philosophical Letters had been condemned and burned in Paris, and a warrant was out for his arrest. He fled to a crumbling chateau at Cirey, on the edge of Champagne. It belonged to the husband of his lover, Emilie, Marquise du Chatelet. The Marquis was usually away with his regiment and was remarkably tolerant. Voltaire paid for the repairs. Emilie arrived with hundreds of boxes. Together they turned a falling house into one of the liveliest places in Europe.

They filled it with books, a physics laboratory, telescopes and a little theatre under the roof. Guests describe late suppers and talk that ran from Newton to gossip to verse. Madame de Graffigny, who stayed through the winter of 1738, wrote letters full of their life: Emilie singing opera, Voltaire reading his new tragedy aloud, plays acted in the attic theatre, quarrels that flared up over dinner and were forgotten by the next evening. They argued all the time. And they loved it.

The sweetest game of all was secret. In 1737 the Academie des sciences, France's great society of scientists, announced a prize for the best essay on the nature and spread of fire. Voltaire set to work in the laboratory, heating iron and weighing it. Emilie followed his work and disagreed with his conclusions. Saying nothing, she began her own essay. She wrote at night so he would not know, sleeping, she later said, about an hour a night for a month, and plunging her hands into iced water to stay awake.

Picture it: a woman at a desk in the sleeping house, her hands cold to the wrist, her pen still moving.

Neither of them won; the great Leonhard Euler took a share of the prize. But when Voltaire learned what she had done, he was not hurt. He was delighted, and he helped to have her essay published beside his own. The Academy printed both in 1739, the first time it had published a work by a woman.

Their love changed over fifteen years and cooled into friendship; both took other lovers. When Emilie died in 1749, days after giving birth, Voltaire was shattered. In a letter to Frederick of Prussia he called her a great man whose only fault was being a woman: a clumsy compliment of its age, and a sincere one.

Two fires, then. One in the laboratory, and one that burned for fifteen years.
tales.reveals: Their sparring was a form of respect: each believed the other could take the hit and return it. The secret essay was a playful challenge between equals, and Voltaire's delight at being outplayed is the mark of a lover who wants an opponent, not an audience.

tales.title: The Merry War
tales.who: Beatrice and Benedick
tales.source: William Shakespeare, Much Ado About Nothing
tales.tale:
A messenger comes to Messina with news that the soldiers are returning from the wars, and before Benedick has even arrived, Beatrice is mocking him. She asks after 'Signior Mountanto', and how many men he has killed, since she promised to eat all of his killing. The messenger is puzzled. Her uncle Leonato explains: there is a kind of merry war between Signior Benedick and her. They never meet but there's a skirmish of wit between them.

Then Benedick walks in, and the skirmish begins at once. 'I wonder that you will still be talking, Signior Benedick,' she says. 'Nobody marks you.' He bows. 'What, my dear Lady Disdain! Are you yet living?' They trade insults the way fencers trade touches, each one quicker than the last, until he walks off with the final word and she remarks that he always ends with a jade's trick, the trick of a worn-out horse.

Everyone in Messina can see what the two of them will not admit. So their friends set a trap. Benedick, hiding in an arbour, a shady seat in the garden, overhears the men saying that Beatrice is secretly dying of love for him. Beatrice, crouched behind a hedge of honeysuckle, overhears the women saying the same of him. Each steps out of hiding changed. Benedick, who swore he would die a bachelor, decides that the world must be peopled.

But the play does not let them stay in the game. At a wedding, Beatrice's cousin Hero is falsely accused and shamed at the altar. In the empty church afterwards, among the cold stones, Beatrice weeps. Benedick has no jokes left. He says: 'I do love nothing in the world so well as you: is not that strange?' She answers in the same strange, honest key, and then makes a terrible demand to prove it. The war of wit becomes a test of loyalty, and he chooses her side.

At the end, they are caught out by their own love sonnets, written in secret and found by their friends. They try one last round of sparring, for old times' sake, the blades flashing one more time. Benedick ends it the only way he can: 'Peace! I will stop your mouth', and kisses her.

The war is over. Both sides have won.
tales.reveals: Their banter was the shape their attraction took while they were too proud to name it. But play alone was not enough: the turning point is the moment the jokes stop and they speak plainly. The best teasing is a prelude to sincerity, not a substitute for it.

practice: Give a woman a teasing nickname rooted in something you admire about her, and let her give you one back.
Argue a playful position you do not hold ('Cats are clearly superior beings') and see if she will spar. Laugh when you lose.
Invent a private ritual or game: a running bet, a recurring question, a word that means something only to the two of you.
Mark your teasing as play with tone, smile and touch, and watch her face: if it lands as hurt, stop and say so warmly.
principles.shadow: Teasing that targets insecurities, humiliates in front of others, or never stops when asked is not play but contempt in a mask. The rule of all good games holds: both must be free to play, and either can call time.

principles.title: Name what others miss
principles.motto: Tell her the true thing about herself that no one else has noticed.
principles.essence: Most people are looked at all day and seen almost never. Notice the quality someone hides, or has stopped believing in, the writer inside the queen, the poet inside the soldier, and name it plainly. To be truly seen is one of the strongest pulls a person can feel.
principles.depth: Psychologists Harry Reis and Phillip Shaver (1988) placed 'perceived partner responsiveness' at the heart of intimacy: we draw close to people who make us feel understood, validated and cared for, and of the three, being understood comes first. William Swann's self-verification theory (from 1983 onward) adds a twist: people seek partners who see them as they see themselves, and can feel uneasy with praise that does not fit. Yet Sandra Murray, John Holmes and Dale Griffin (1996) found that couples are happiest when each sees the other slightly more generously than the other sees themselves. Put together, the art is precise: name something real, and name its best version. That is the difference between seeing and flattery. Flattery is generic and could be said to anyone; seeing is specific and could only be said to this person. Philosophers have called this kind of attention a moral act. Simone Weil, in a 1942 letter to Joe Bousquet, wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Iris Murdoch defined love as the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real. Martin Buber, in I and Thou (1923), described the moment when a person stops being an object of use and becomes a 'Thou' encountered whole. To be seen that way is to be called into existence.

tales.title: The Faery and the Primroses
tales.who: Benjamin Disraeli and Queen Victoria
tales.source: The letters of Queen Victoria; G. W. E. Russell, Collections and Recollections (1898); the biographies of Robert Blake and Christopher Hibbert
tales.tale:
A widow in black, far from London, and a man who looked at her and saw more. When Benjamin Disraeli first became Prime Minister in February 1868, Queen Victoria had been a widow for six years. She had spent most of them in black, withdrawn from London, mourning Prince Albert so completely that the newspapers grumbled about an invisible monarch. Her ministers gave her correct respect and endless papers. Her previous Prime Minister, William Gladstone, was brilliant and honourable, and she disliked him. He spoke to her, she is supposed to have complained, as if she were a public meeting.

Disraeli saw something else. He saw a lonely woman of fifty who had been, with Albert, a working partner in government, and who missed being asked, told and amused. He saw, too, a woman who had just published a book. In 1868 her Leaves from the Journal of Our Life in the Highlands appeared, and Disraeli, a novelist himself, is said to have begun remarks to her with 'We authors, Ma'am'. Whether or not those exact words were spoken, the attitude was real. He treated her as a fellow writer, a fellow worker, and a woman.

His letters to her were unlike anything a Prime Minister had sent before: bright, gossipy accounts of debates in the Commons, little sketches of who had spoken well and who had fumbled, written to entertain as much as inform. He called her the Faery, after Spenser's long poem The Faerie Queene. After his first audience she wrote to her eldest daughter that he was full of poetry, romance and chivalry, and that he had knelt to kiss her hand in loving loyalty and faith.

She began to send him primroses from the woods at Osborne and Windsor. Small pale flowers of early spring, sent from her hand to his. In 1876 he gave her the title Empress of India. When he died in April 1881, custom did not allow her to attend the funeral, but she sent a wreath of primroses with a card in her own hand: 'His favourite flowers'. Days later she went to his grave at Hughenden.

Disraeli was frank about his methods. He told the poet Matthew Arnold, according to G. W. E. Russell, that everyone likes flattery, and with royalty you should lay it on with a trowel. But flattery alone does not explain thirteen years of devotion.

What held her was simpler. He had noticed what the widow in black still was.
tales.reveals: Disraeli's compliments worked because they were anchored in true perception: she was a writer, a worker and a woman who wanted to be addressed as all three. Flattery spread on a wall of real insight sticks; flattery on nothing slides off. His trowel is the warning; his seeing is the lesson.

tales.title: The Voice Beneath the Balcony
tales.who: Cyrano de Bergerac and Roxane
tales.source: Edmond Rostand, Cyrano de Bergerac, Act III (1897); loosely based on the real Savinien de Cyrano de Bergerac (1619 to 1655)
tales.tale:
Night in Paris, a window lit above a dark street, and a man hiding in the shadow beneath it. Roxane is clever, and she knows it. She belongs to the circle of the precieuses, the women of Paris who prize a beautiful sentence the way others prize a jewel. She has fallen for a handsome young cadet, Christian, and he for her. But Christian has a problem: he cannot speak to her. Her cousin Cyrano loves her desperately and believes his enormous nose makes him unlovable. He has been writing Christian's letters for him, and Roxane is enchanted by them.

One night Christian insists on wooing her alone. He stands beneath her balcony and says, 'I love you.' She waits. He says it again. That is the theme, Roxane tells him; now embroider it. He tries: he loves her very much. She is bored, then cross, and she shuts the window.

Cyrano, watching from the shadows, cannot bear it. He pushes Christian under the balcony, hides himself in the dark beneath, and begins to speak in a low voice, as if he were Christian. At first he stumbles. Then the words come. Freed by the darkness from the face he is ashamed of, he says everything he has kept inside for years. He does not praise her eyes or her hair like every other suitor. He speaks to her mind, her taste, her hunger for something rarer than compliments. Asked what a kiss is, he answers with a speech that has been loved ever since: an oath sworn a little closer, a promise sealed, a rosy dot placed on the i of the verb to love.

Roxane, who has been admired all her life, is at last truly seen. She calls Christian up to claim his kiss. Cyrano stays in the dark below.

Later, at the siege of Arras, she tells Christian that she no longer loves him for his beauty but for his soul, and would love him even if he were ugly. Christian understands at once: she loves Cyrano.

Fifteen years after Christian's death, in a convent garden at dusk, Cyrano reads aloud his last letter, though it is too dark to read. The light is gone. The words are not. And Roxane realises whose voice it always was.
tales.reveals: Roxane was not won by beauty or by declarations, but by a voice that understood what she valued and spoke directly to it. The tragedy is the other half of the lesson: Cyrano saw her perfectly but hid himself, and to be loved, the one who sees must also step into the light and be seen.

practice: This week, before complimenting anyone, ask yourself: could I say this to anyone else? If so, find something only true of them.
Notice a quality a woman undervalues in herself (her patience, her eye for colour, the way she listens) and name it plainly, once, without fuss.
Ask about the part of a woman's life others overlook: the project she gave up, the language she half speaks, the city she misses.
Remember a small detail she mentioned in passing and bring it back days later. Proof of attention is more persuasive than praise.
principles.shadow: Seeing becomes manipulation when it is used to find soft spots to exploit, or when flattery imitates insight to gain something. Name only what you truly perceive, and never use what you see in a woman as leverage against her.

principles.title: Let them feel chosen
principles.motto: Choose her clearly, and let her know it was not by chance.
principles.essence: We are drawn to those who are drawn to us, but only when their wanting is particular. Liking handed out to everyone means little; liking that singles someone out, for reasons only they could earn, is hard to resist. Let people feel chosen: specifically, sincerely, and by someone who chooses with care.
principles.depth: One of the oldest findings in the study of attraction is reciprocity: we like those who like us. Carl Backman and Paul Secord showed in 1959 that people told a group member liked them came to like that person in return. But the effect has a condition. Elaine Walster and colleagues (1973), testing the folk wisdom about playing hard to get, found that men most preferred a woman who was selectively hard to get: keen on them, cool towards others. Paul Eastwick, Eli Finkel and colleagues confirmed it in speed-dating research (2007): people who expressed interest in everyone were desired less, while a person's unique interest in one partner was strongly returned. Elliot Aronson and Darwyn Linder (1965) added that esteem which grows, which seems to be won, can count for more than esteem given from the start, though later studies found that gain effect fragile. The common thread is discernment: praise matters when it comes from someone who could have withheld it. Aristotle said as much in the Nicomachean Ethics (Book VIII): friendship requires goodwill that is mutual and known to both. Montaigne, asked why he loved his friend Etienne de La Boetie, could only answer: because it was he, because it was I. To feel chosen is to feel that kind of because.

tales.title: I Love You Too
tales.who: Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett
tales.where: 50 Wimpole Street, London, and New Cross
tales.source: The Letters of Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett Barrett, 1845 to 1846 (published 1899)
tales.tale:
A darkened room at the back of a London house, and a woman who almost never left it. In 1844 Elizabeth Barrett was the most celebrated woman poet in England. She was thirty eight, an invalid since her youth, living in a back bedroom at 50 Wimpole Street under the rule of a father who forbade any of his children to marry. Her new volume of Poems had made her famous. Tucked into one of them, a long ballad called 'Lady Geraldine's Courtship', was a line of praise for a younger poet whose work few people yet admired: Robert Browning. His pamphlet series Bells and Pomegranates was, she wrote, like a pomegranate which, cut deep down the middle, shows a heart within blood-tinctured, of a veined humanity.

Browning, thirty two and living with his parents in New Cross, read it. A mutual friend, her cousin John Kenyon, urged him to write to her. On 10 January 1845 he did, and his first sentence was: 'I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett.' He went on to praise particular lines, with the care of someone who had truly read them. Then, near the end of that first letter, he wrote something astonishing: 'I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart, and I love you too.'

She replied the next day: 'I thank you, dear Mr Browning, from the bottom of my heart.' She did not take his words for a declaration of love; she took them as a poet's generosity. But a correspondence had begun. Over the next twenty months they wrote to each other almost every day, nearly six hundred letters in all, back and forth across London like a thread pulled slowly tight. In May 1845 he was allowed to visit. He came again and again, always on fixed afternoons, so that her father would not notice.

She had been chosen by a man who had first been chosen by her, in a line of verse, when hardly anyone else had noticed him. That double choosing gave her courage.

On 12 September 1846 they were married secretly at St Marylebone Parish Church. A week later she left Wimpole Street with her maid and her dog Flush and fled with him to Italy. Her father never spoke to her again. Her health improved. She wrote the Sonnets from the Portuguese for him, including the one that begins 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.'
tales.reveals: Browning's letter worked because it was specific: he loved particular lines, for particular reasons, and that made his warmth credible. And it answered her own earlier praise of him. Two people who had each singled the other out found the courage, together, to break out of a locked room.

tales.title: The Overheard Opinion
tales.who: Elliot Aronson and Darwyn Linder, and their volunteers
tales.source: Aronson and Linder, 'Gain and loss of esteem as determinants of interpersonal attractiveness', Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 1965
tales.tale:
A thin wall, and on the other side of it, a voice talking about you. A female student arrives at the laboratory and is told she will help run an experiment. Her job, the experimenter explains, is to hold a series of short conversations with another student, who is supposedly the real subject. Between conversations, the other student will be interviewed by the experimenter, and through a thin wall our volunteer will be able to overhear what is said.

What she overhears, again and again, is the other student describing her.

The other student is in fact working with the experimenters, and her comments follow a script. There are seven conversations, and so seven verdicts, and Elliot Aronson and Darwyn Linder designed four different patterns. Some volunteers heard only warm things from beginning to end: she seems intelligent, interesting, someone I would like. Some heard only cold things: dull, ordinary, not my type. Some heard warmth that slowly chilled into criticism. And some heard the reverse: an early judgement that was cool, even dismissive, which thawed meeting by meeting, like ice in a spring sun, until by the end the other student said she really liked her.

At the end, each volunteer was asked how much she liked the student she had been talking with.

You would guess that those praised from start to finish would like her best. They did not. The highest liking went to the student whose opinion had been won over: cool at first, then warmer and warmer. And the lowest went, by a small margin, to the student who had liked her at first and then gone off her, lower even than the one who had been unkind throughout.

Aronson called it the gain and loss effect. Praise that changes in our favour, he suggested, feels earned. It comes from someone who clearly has taste and judgement, who was not handing out kind words to everyone, and who changed their mind because of who we turned out to be.
