Later research found the gain effect weaker and less steady than this first study suggested, and it should not be treated as a law.

But the heart of it has held up well. Being liked by someone who chooses carefully matters far more than being liked by someone who likes everybody.
tales.reveals: What pleased the volunteers was not warmth itself but the sense of having been chosen by someone discerning. To feel that someone's regard grew as they came to know you is to feel seen and selected, which is why indiscriminate praise is so much weaker than particular, earned esteem.

practice: When you feel drawn to a woman, tell her what in particular drew you: the remark she made, the way she handled a situation. Specific beats lavish.
Let your interest be visibly selective: give your fullest attention to the one you are courting, rather than spreading the same charm around the whole room.
Tell a woman how your view of her has grown since you met ('At first I thought you were reserved; now I think you are the funniest person I know').
Write one short letter or message whose only purpose is to say why you chose her, and ask for nothing in return.
principles.shadow: Do not stage coldness in order to turn on warmth later; a manufactured 'gain' is a lie and is usually discovered. Choose people honestly, and never make anyone audition for affection you have already decided to give.

principles.title: Desire lives in the gap
principles.motto: What is promised and not yet given glows brightest in the mind.
principles.essence: Desire feeds not only on what you receive but on what you are waiting to receive. Leave room between the promise and its keeping, and let the other person's imagination do its gilding. Then keep the promise: anticipation is a loan that must be repaid.
principles.depth: The brain treats expectation as a pleasure in itself. Wolfram Schultz's recordings of dopamine neurons in the 1990s showed them firing not only at a reward but at the cue that predicts it, and Schultz and colleagues later found a sustained glow of activity while the outcome was still uncertain. The economist George Loewenstein (1987) asked people what they would pay to kiss the film star of their choice: they valued the kiss more if it came in three days than at once, because three days of savoring were part of the gift. A Dutch study of holidaymakers (Nawijn and colleagues, 2010) found that the happiness boost came mostly before the trip, not after it. Stendhal named the mental side of this in 1822: crystallization, the mind's habit of decorating an absent beloved with every perfection it can find. The poet and classicist Anne Carson, in Eros the Bittersweet (1986), argues that eros is by nature a lack, alive in the space between lover and beloved; Sappho's word for it was glukupikron, sweetbitter. Roland Barthes, in A Lover's Discourse (1977), observed that the lover is the one who waits. The art is to make that waiting delicious rather than anxious: a horizon, not a hole.

tales.title: The Bough in the Salt Mine
tales.who: Stendhal (Henri Beyle) and Matilde Dembowski
tales.where: Milan, Volterra and the salt mines near Salzburg
tales.source: Stendhal, De l'amour (1822), Book I, ch. 2, and the fragment 'The Salzburg Bough'; his journals and letters
tales.tale:
Milan, 1818. Henri Beyle, a stout former officer of Napoleon's army who would later sign his books Stendhal, meets Matilde Dembowski. She lives apart from her husband, a general born in Poland. She is grave and clever, admired in the city's free-thinking drawing rooms. He falls at once, and all the way. She lets him call, but not too often. She listens, but she promises nothing. For three years he lives on the empty days between visits, counting each one.

In June 1819 the waiting is too much. She has gone to Volterra, where her sons are at school, and he follows her across Tuscany. Foolishly, he puts on a pair of green spectacles so she will not know him in the street. She knows him at once. She is hurt, she tells him so in writing, and the visits grow rarer still.

What do you do with a love that is given nothing to eat? Beyle did what writers do. He studied it. Near Salzburg, he wrote, miners throw a leafless winter bough deep into an old working of the salt mine. Two or three months later they draw it out, and it is covered in shining crystals. The smallest twigs, no thicker than the claw of a titmouse (a tiny bird), glitter with countless diamonds. The plain branch can no longer be seen.

That, he said, is what a lover's mind does while the loved one is away. Every good thing you find in her, every good thing you guess at, every good thing you dream up, settles on her like salt. He called it crystallization, and he named its steps: admiration; the thought of how sweet a kiss would be; hope; the birth of love; a first crystallization. Then doubt, which sends the lover back down into the dark to grow a second, harder coat of jewels.

He left Milan in 1821, under the eye of the Austrian police, in despair. In 1822 he published De l'amour, which, as he later joked, sold almost nothing for years. Matilde died in 1825. He never won her. The book is partly the record of a waiting never repaid.

Yet the image outlived them both. Anyone who has waited three days for a letter knows the bough. The crystals are real pleasures, but they are made in the dark, from the lover's own salt. And if love is to be more than a mine, one day the branch must be drawn up into the light and loved as wood.
tales.reveals: Anticipation is a workshop where the imagination makes the beloved more precious than any real person can be. Stendhal shows both its power and its danger: crystals grown on absence alone can keep you in love with someone you barely know. Use the gap to deepen desire, then close it, so that love can meet the real branch.

tales.title: The Diary of Johannes
tales.who: Johannes the Seducer and Cordelia Wahl (fictional); Søren Kierkegaard and Regine Olsen
tales.when: 1843 (written after Kierkegaard broke his engagement in 1841)
tales.source: Søren Kierkegaard, Either/Or, Part I, 'The Seducer's Diary' (1843), published under the pseudonym Victor Eremita. A work of fiction.
tales.tale:
In February 1843 a thick book appeared in Copenhagen. It was called Either/Or. Its editor, who called himself Victor Eremita, said he had found the papers inside an old writing desk he had bought. It was a story, of course, and the whole book is a work of fiction. The last of those papers was a diary kept by a young man named Johannes. It is one of the coldest love stories ever written, because its hero is not in love at all. He is in love with waiting.

Johannes first sees Cordelia Wahl, a young girl, in the street. He does not go to her. He learns her habits. He finds the house where she lives with her aunt. He lets the weeks pass. He does not want a quick win, he writes, but the interesting: a feeling that ripens slowly, under his hand. So he becomes a fixture in the aunt's parlour. He talks dryly with the aunt about farming and prices, and he barely looks at Cordelia, who begins to wonder why this clever man ignores her.

Every move is made to widen the gap. He steers a dull young suitor toward her, so that next to the dull one he seems a mystery. He becomes engaged to her, then quietly teaches her to find the engagement small and ordinary, until she breaks it herself, to be free for something grander. He writes her letters full of longing, and keeps himself away. In the diary he notes her moods the way a gardener notes the weather, enjoying each stage of her waiting more than he will enjoy its end.

The end comes in a single night in the country. The diary closes coldly: it is over now, and he wants never to see her again. Cordelia, the editor tells us, wrote him letters that came back unopened.

Kierkegaard knew something about stepping back. In 1841 he had broken his engagement to Regine Olsen, a young woman he loved, and some readers think he wrote the diary partly to make her believe him a scoundrel, and so set her free. Whatever his reasons, he placed Johannes in what he called the aesthetic sphere: a life lived for the interesting moment, a life that can never promise, because a promise would end the suspense.

Read the diary as a mirror, and as a warning. Johannes understands waiting better than almost anyone in books. What he never understands is that he was the one going hungry.
tales.reveals: Anticipation can be turned into a weapon: a way of steering someone else's longing while risking nothing yourself. Kierkegaard's seducer shows how the gap, used as control rather than as invitation, empties both people. Build anticipation toward a meeting you truly intend, never as an end in itself.

practice: Make one plan a few days ahead instead of tonight, and name one vivid detail of it ('the bench by the river at dusk, bring a coat') so the other person has something to picture.
End a good conversation or evening while it is still rising, with a warm line about next time, rather than letting it run on until it fades.
Send a short message that opens a door without walking through it: a story you promise to tell in person, a book you will bring when you meet.
Notice your own crystallization: write down three qualities you have assumed about someone you are drawn to, and look for real evidence of them the next time you meet.
principles.shadow: Anticipation curdles when the promise is never kept, or when delay becomes a lever to keep someone anxious and waiting on you. Make every gap lead somewhere real, and never stage another person's longing for your own amusement.

principles.title: A little not-knowing
principles.motto: Let her wonder about your next move, never about your goodwill.
principles.essence: A mind that is not quite sure keeps returning to the question. Leave a little room for wondering about what you think and what you will do, and the other person will think of you more. But uncertainty is a spice, not a meal: beneath it there must be steady warmth.
principles.depth: In 2011 Erin Whitchurch, Timothy Wilson and Daniel Gilbert told women that men had viewed and rated their profiles; those left unsure how much the men liked them thought about the men more and found them more attractive than women told the men liked them best. Wilson's earlier work on the 'pleasure paradox' (Wilson, Centerbar, Kermer and Gilbert, 2005) suggests why: we explain events in order to settle them, and once settled they fade, while an open question keeps a pleasant feeling alive. George Loewenstein's information-gap theory of curiosity (1994) adds that a small, noticeable gap in knowledge creates an itch to close it. Hold these findings lightly. The 2011 study rested on one small sample of 47 students, and a large body of research finds reciprocal liking among the strongest causes of attraction. Uncertainty that runs long breeds anxiety rather than desire, especially in people with an anxious attachment style. Literature knew both faces. In Proust's Swann's Way (1913), Swann falls fully in love with Odette on the night he cannot find her in the cafés of Paris, and from then on his love is a long fever of doubt. Light uncertainty about details invites; uncertainty about your basic regard wounds.

tales.title: He Loves Me, He Loves Me Not
tales.who: Erin Whitchurch, Timothy Wilson, Daniel Gilbert and 47 student volunteers
tales.source: Whitchurch, Wilson and Gilbert, 'He loves me, he loves me not...: Uncertainty can increase romantic attraction', Psychological Science, 2011
tales.tale:
A quiet room at the University of Virginia. A student sits before a screen. She has been told this is a study of how people form first impressions on Facebook, and that her own profile has been shown to male students at other universities, who rated how much they thought they would like her. Now it is her turn. Four young men appear one by one: a photograph, some interests, a few lines about music and weekends.

She is one of 47 women in an experiment published in 2011 by Erin Whitchurch, Timothy Wilson and Daniel Gilbert. (Think of her as a composite. The paper reports groups, not names.) Some women were told these four men had rated them among the highest of all the women they had seen. Some were told the men had rated them about average. And some, the group our student is in, were told only that the men were either among those who liked her most or among those who rated her average. The researchers would not say which.

The men did not exist. The researchers had made them up. But the feelings were real enough to measure. At several points the women were asked how much the men had been on their minds. Our student, unsure, kept drifting back to the four faces. Did the one with the guitar like her? Had the serious one ranked her low? She turned the question over and over, the way you turn a smooth stone in your pocket.

When the answers came in, the pattern was clear. Women told the men liked them best did like those men back, just as years of research would predict: we tend to like people who like us. But the women left not knowing liked the men even more, and thought about them more often. Not knowing had kept the men alive in their minds.

'He loves me, he loves me not,' the title of the paper began, borrowing the old game of pulling petals from a daisy. The game is only exciting while petals remain.

But the limits matter as much as the finding. These were brief, made-up meetings with strangers, not real relationships. The group was small, and no one has turned the result into a settled law. Not knowing seems to sharpen early interest. Nobody has shown that it builds a love that lasts.
tales.reveals: A light, early uncertainty keeps a person in the mind, because the mind cannot finish thinking about an open question. But the study captures a spark among strangers, not a bond: reciprocity remains the ground, and uncertainty is only the weather passing over it.

tales.title: Remember Me
tales.who: Lady Caroline Lamb and Lord Byron
tales.where: London: Melbourne House in Whitehall and Byron's rooms in St James's Street
tales.source: Lady Caroline Lamb's journal and letters; Byron's letters and his poem 'Remember thee! remember thee!' (1813); Fiona MacCarthy, Byron: Life and Legend (2002); Paul Douglass, Lady Caroline Lamb (2004)
tales.tale:
London, March 1812, and the whole city is talking about one young lord, the man who wrote Childe Harold's Pilgrimage. At a party, Lady Caroline Lamb, wife of William Lamb, slender, restless and brilliant at twenty-six, looks at the crowd pressing around Byron and, by her own account, turns on her heel without being introduced. That night, as tradition has it, she writes in her journal the words that have followed him ever since: mad, bad and dangerous to know.

Her turning away caught him. When they met days later at Holland House, he asked, as she later told it, 'This offer was made to you before; may I ask why you rejected it?' Within weeks they could not be parted. He came to Melbourne House almost every day. Page boys ran between them with notes. They quarreled and made up in the same afternoon. For a few months they were the most watched pair in London.

Then Byron began to cool. He did not end it cleanly. A warm letter, then a cold one. He stayed away, then came back. He let her hope. Caroline, who had always lived on fire, could not bear the not-knowing. She came to his rooms in St James's Street dressed as a page boy. She sent him locks of her hair and begged for his. In the late summer of 1812 her family took her to Ireland. She wrote to him from there, and he, by then with Lady Oxford, sent a letter ending it, which she later flung before the world.

The doubt that had once been a thrill now ate her alive. In July 1813, at a ball at Lady Heathcote's, after sharp words with Byron, she cut herself with a knife or broken glass, and the scandal filled every drawing room. One day, finding him out, she wrote 'Remember me!' in a book on his table. He answered in verse, cruelly: 'Remember thee! remember thee! / Till Lethe quench life's burning stream, / Remorse and shame shall cling to thee, / And haunt thee like a feverish dream!'

In 1816 she put him in a novel, Glenarvon, as a beautiful, faithless villain. She never fully found her peace again. In 1824, it is said, she met his funeral procession by chance on the road, and fell ill.

Their story is often told as her madness. It is better read as what happens when one person keeps another forever unsure. A spark becomes a wound.
tales.reveals: Uncertainty that delights in the first weeks becomes torment when it lasts, and when it concerns the heart rather than the details. Byron's blowing hot and cold kept Caroline hooked and destroyed her peace; the lesson is to let mystery play on the surface while making your basic regard, or your goodbye, unmistakable.

practice: Do not explain every feeling the moment it arises: let a compliment stand on its own, without a follow-up asking how it landed.
Keep one or two things about your plans or past to reveal later, and say so lightly: 'Ask me about that another time.'
Let the rhythm of your contact vary a little instead of replying with clockwork speed, while never leaving a sincere question unanswered.
If you are cooling toward a woman, say so clearly and kindly within the week; do not leave her living in the 'maybe'.
principles.shadow: Deliberate hot and cold is a slot-machine tactic that breeds anxiety, not love, and it preys most on the insecure. Let her wonder about your next move, never about your respect or your honesty.

principles.title: Withhold to heighten
principles.motto: Be lavish with warmth and sparing with access.
principles.essence: We value what is rare, and most of all what is rare and chosen. Be generous with warmth but selective with your time, your body and your inner rooms, so that what you give carries weight. Withholding works only when it comes from genuine standards, never from a game of refusal.
principles.depth: Scarcity raises value. In a 1975 study by Stephen Worchel, Jerry Lee and Akanbi Adewole, people rated identical cookies as more desirable when they came from a jar holding two rather than ten, and more desirable still when the jar had just been emptied down to two. Jack Brehm's theory of psychological reactance (1966) explains part of it: when a freedom is threatened, we want the threatened thing more. Robert Cialdini made scarcity one of the principles of his book Influence (1984). But attraction is subtler than cookies. When Elaine Walster and colleagues tested the old advice to 'play hard to get' (1973), they found that men did not prefer women who were hard for everyone to get. The most attractive women were those who seemed selectively hard to get: warm toward the chooser and cool toward his rivals. Scarcity, in other words, must feel like choice, not rejection. Ovid caught the mechanism two thousand years ago: nitimur in vetitum, we strain toward the forbidden (Amores III.4). The same line holds a warning, since what we want only because it is forbidden we may not truly want. The healthy form of scarcity is simply having a life, standards and limits of your own.

tales.title: Henry Seeks No Other
tales.who: Anne Boleyn and Henry VIII
tales.where: The English court at Greenwich and London; Hever Castle in Kent
tales.source: Henry VIII's seventeen surviving love letters to Anne Boleyn, Vatican Library (Vat. Lat. 3731); Eric Ives, The Life and Death of Anne Boleyn (2004)
tales.tale:
Around 1526 the King of England was thirty-five years old and had been married for seventeen years to Catherine of Aragon. Then he fell in love with one of her ladies. Anne Boleyn was not the beauty of the court. She was dark and quick, polished first at the court of Margaret of Austria in Mechelen and then in France, and she talked with a wit that made men lean closer. The king was used to having what he wanted. He had already had Anne's sister Mary as his mistress.

Anne would not be his mistress. Her letters are lost. His survive, seventeen of them, which somehow ended up in the Vatican Library, where they still lie. In them we can watch a king meet the word no.

In one, written in French, he complains that for above a whole year he has been struck with the dart of love, and still does not know if he has failed or found a place in her heart. If she will give herself to him, he offers to make her his only mistress, 'rejecting from thought and affection all others save yourself'. She did not accept. She went home to her family's house at Hever in Kent, and he wrote again, aching at the distance.

Then she sent him a gift: a jewel showing a ship, and in it a lone girl tossed about on the waves. Henry read it as a kind of yielding, a woman adrift who would trust herself to him, though not as a mistress. He thanked her for the 'fine interpretation' and the humble promise it held, and swore to be hers. He signed some letters with her initials drawn inside a heart, and the words 'autre ne cherche' set around his own: Henry seeks no other.

For some six years she held the line, and her no reshaped a kingdom. To make her his wife, Henry broke with the Church of Rome. They married in secret in January 1533. She was crowned that June. Their daughter Elizabeth was born in September. Less than three years later, on 19 May 1536, Anne was beheaded at the Tower of London, on charges most historians believe were false.

Was her refusal a plan, or a shield? She had seen what became of her sister. Probably both. What is clear is that the closed door made a great hunger, and that a hunger built on the chase did not know what to do once the chase was over.
tales.reveals: Anne's 'no' turned a passing royal appetite into the most consequential courtship in English history. Scarcity heightened desire immensely, but the tale also shows its limit: longing fed mainly by refusal can sour once it is satisfied, so what is withheld must be worth more than the withholding.

tales.title: The Laurel
tales.who: Apollo and Daphne
tales.where: The valley of the river Peneus, Thessaly
tales.source: Greek myth, told by Ovid, Metamorphoses I.452 to 567; later carved by Bernini (1622 to 1625, Galleria Borghese, Rome)
tales.tale:
Apollo, proud from killing the serpent Python with his arrows, laughed at Cupid for carrying a bow at all. What business had a boy with the weapons of a god? Cupid said nothing. He flew to the shadowed peak of Parnassus and drew two arrows. One was gold and sharp, and it lit love. The other was blunt and tipped with lead, and it put love to flight. The gold he shot into Apollo. The lead he shot into Daphne, daughter of the river god Peneus.

Daphne already wanted nothing of men. She ran through the woods like a follower of Diana, her hair tied loosely with a ribbon, and had begged her father to let her stay unmarried forever. Now the god of light saw her, and burned, Ovid says, as dry stubble burns after the harvest. He admired her eyes like stars, her lips, her fingers, her arms. And whatever was hidden, Ovid adds, he imagined to be better still.

She ran. He followed, and as he ran he talked. Stop, he called, I am no enemy. I am no shepherd, no rough herdsman. Delphi is mine. Jupiter is my father. I am the lord of music, of prophecy, of healing. Then a line that is almost funny, and chilling: run more slowly, I beg you, and I will chase more slowly.

None of it mattered. Every word of his boasting was true, and none of it answered the one thing she had said, which was her running. Her flight only made her lovelier to him. The wind bared her limbs and streamed her hair behind her. Love gave him speed. His breath was on her neck.

At the river she cried to her father to destroy the beauty that had brought her harm. A heavy numbness took her limbs. Bark closed over her breast. Her hair became leaves, her arms branches, her quick feet roots. Apollo laid his hand on the trunk and felt her heart still trembling under the new bark. He kissed the wood, and the wood shrank from his kisses.

Even then he would not let go. 'Since you cannot be my wife,' he said, 'you shall at least be my tree.' He crowned his hair and his lyre with laurel, and so the laurel became the leaf of winners.

This is myth, and Ovid tells it tenderly. Bernini later froze the moment in marble. But the shape of the story is plain. What Apollo took for a prize held back was a no.
tales.reveals: The myth is the hinge between scarcity and its corruption. Daphne's absence fed Apollo's desire, but her absence was a refusal, and he treated it as a challenge. True scarcity is a person's own choice to hold something back for now; a 'no' is not a game to be won.

practice: Keep one evening this week for something you love doing alone, and do not cancel it for a new invitation; offer another night instead.
Let an early meeting end with something still ahead of you both, a kiss, a story or a place, rather than giving everything at once.
Be warm and specific with the person you are interested in and pleasantly ordinary with everyone else, so that your attention reads as a choice.
When a woman holds back, take her at her word: step back, stay friendly, and leave her free to come forward if she wishes.
principles.shadow: Manufactured scarcity, from fake busyness to calculated coldness, is manipulation, and it eventually reads as contempt. Never treat a woman's reluctance as a scarcity to overcome: her 'no' ends the chase.

principles.title: Walls feed the fire
principles.motto: A shared obstacle turns two people into a conspiracy.
principles.essence: Love grows urgent when something stands in its way: distance, disapproval, time, a rule. An obstacle faced together gives you secrets, signals and the delicious sense of being allies against the world. But watch for the moment the fire begins to love the wall more than the person behind it.
principles.depth: In 1972 Richard Driscoll, Keith Davis and Milton Lipetz surveyed couples in Colorado and reported a 'Romeo and Juliet effect': the more parents interfered, the more in love the couples said they were. It became a textbook classic. It also failed to hold. When H. Colleen Sinclair and colleagues revisited it in 2014 with a much larger sample, they found the reverse: approval from parents and friends predicted more love and commitment, and disapproval predicted less, a pattern called the social network effect. What does seem sturdy is narrower. Jack Brehm's reactance makes forbidden things more vivid, and shared adversity creates a strong sense of us. Freud, in his 1912 essay on the universal tendency to debasement in love, wrote that an obstacle is needed to heighten libido, and that where natural resistances were lacking, people have always built conventional ones in order to enjoy love. The Swiss writer Denis de Rougemont, in Love in the Western World (1939), went further: the Tristan legend, he argued, taught Europe to love passion itself, and its lovers secretly needed the barriers that kept them apart, even unto death. Use obstacles as play and alliance, not as the whole engine. A love that needs a wall to burn will keep looking for new walls.

tales.title: The Crack in the Wall
tales.who: Pyramus and Thisbe
tales.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses IV.55 to 166, told by one of the daughters of Minyas
tales.tale:
In Babylon, the city that Semiramis, so the story goes, ringed with walls of baked brick, two houses stood side by side. In one lived Pyramus, the handsomest young man of the East. In the other, Thisbe, the most admired of its girls. Being neighbours, they met as children. Being near, they fell in love. They would have married, but their fathers forbade it. What the fathers could not forbid, Ovid says, was that both burned the same. And the more the fire was hidden, the hotter it grew.

The wall between the houses had a thin crack, left by the builders and unseen for years. The lovers saw it. What does love not see? They made it a road for their voices, and soft words crossed in murmurs. Often, one on each side, catching each other's breath, they would scold it: 'Jealous wall, why do you stand in the way of lovers? What would it cost you to let us embrace?' And yet, they admitted, they owed it something, for it carried their words to loving ears. At nightfall they said goodbye, and each gave the wall kisses that never reached the other side.

The wall, of course, is what made every whisper precious. In the end it was not enough. They agreed to slip out by night and meet outside the city at the tomb of Ninus, under a tall mulberry tree heavy with snow-white berries, beside a cool spring.

Thisbe came first, veiled, made bold by love. A lioness came to the spring to drink, her jaws bloody from a fresh kill. Thisbe fled into a cave and dropped her veil. The lioness, turning back to the woods, found it and tore it with her bloody mouth. Pyramus came late. He saw the tracks in the dust and the stained veil, and believed the worst. 'One night will destroy two lovers,' he cried, and he drove his sword into his side, and his blood leapt up and darkened the white berries.

Thisbe returned and saw the berries changed. Then she saw him. She called his name. He opened his eyes once, at hers, and closed them. She took the same sword, asking only that their parents lay them in one tomb, and that the tree bear dark fruit in mourning. Gods and parents granted both.

Shakespeare later let his clumsy workmen act this story in A Midsummer Night's Dream, and the audience laughs. The laughter is a kind of wisdom.
tales.reveals: The wall gave Pyramus and Thisbe their secret language, their rituals and their urgency; the obstacle made the love feel enormous. But the same hunger to defeat the wall drove them to a reckless night meeting, and the ending shows how passion fed by barriers can rush past judgment.

tales.title: The Sword Between Them
tales.who: Tristan, Isolde and King Mark of Cornwall
tales.when: legend; first written versions c. 1170 to 1210
tales.where: Cornwall and the forest of Morrois
tales.source: Medieval legend, in the versions of Béroul and Thomas of Britain (both 12th century) and Gottfried von Strassburg (c. 1210); later Richard Wagner's Tristan und Isolde (1865)
tales.tale:
Tristan was sent over the sea to Ireland to bring home a bride for his uncle, King Mark of Cornwall. The bride was Isolde, the golden-haired Irish princess, who had once healed his wounds and once, in Gottfried's telling, nearly killed him in his bath when she found he had slain her uncle. On the voyage home, the legend says, the day was hot and they were thirsty, and a flask was close at hand. It held a love potion, made by Isolde's mother for the wedding night of Isolde and Mark and left in the care of the maid Brangaine. Tristan and Isolde drank it together, and from that moment they could not be apart.

So began a love made almost wholly of walls. She married the king. Tristan served at his court. Every meeting had to be stolen. In an orchard at night beneath a pine, as Béroul tells it, the lovers see in the spring at their feet the face of the king, hidden in the branches above, and turn their meeting into an innocent quarrel for his ears. Lords watched them. A dwarf scattered flour between their beds to catch Tristan's footprints. Each danger seemed to bind them tighter.

At last they fled into the forest of Morrois and lived there a while, poor and hunted. In Béroul's telling, King Mark found them one day asleep in a shelter of leaves, fully clothed, with Tristan's bare sword lying between their bodies. Taking it as a sign they were chaste, the king did not strike. He laid his own sword in place of Tristan's. He slipped his ring onto Isolde's finger. He set his glove in the leaves to shade her face from a ray of sun. When they woke and understood, they were not comforted but afraid, and fled deeper.

In Thomas's version the end comes far from home. Tristan, married to another Isolde, Isolde of the White Hands, is wounded by a poisoned weapon and sends for the first Isolde to heal him. If she comes, the ship will fly a white sail. If not, a black one. His jealous wife sees the white sail and tells him it is black. He dies. Isolde lands, lies down beside him, and dies too.

The writer Denis de Rougemont read the legend as Europe's great confession: the lovers, he argued, wanted each other less than the burning that being apart gave them. Even the sword in the forest was a wall they had raised themselves.
tales.reveals: Tristan and Isolde's love burns brightest exactly where it is most forbidden, and the legend hints that they half needed the walls. A shared obstacle can bind two people fiercely, but if only danger makes you feel alive together, you may be in love with the obstacle and not the person.

practice: Build a small private world with someone: a code word, a look across a crowded room, a ritual only the two of you know.
If you will be apart for a while, give the separation a shape: a date, a countdown, the first thing you will do together when you meet.
Take on a real challenge side by side this week, such as a hard hike or a dinner for friends with a deadline, and notice how it makes you allies.
Ask yourself honestly whether your desire for someone depends on what keeps you apart; imagine the wall gone, and see what remains.
principles.shadow: Do not manufacture walls through secrecy that wounds third parties, or chase people precisely because they are unavailable. Drama is not depth, and a love that needs ever higher walls ends up living in a fortress or a tomb.

principles.title: Seduce at a distance
principles.motto: Ink lets you be your truest self, slowly, in someone else's hands.
principles.essence: A letter, or any carefully made message, lets you give your full attention and your best words at the pace of reflection. Write to be read twice: specific, sensory, honest, in a voice only you could have. Distance becomes an intimate room when words are chosen with care.
principles.depth: Joseph Walther's theory of hyperpersonal communication (1996) found that people writing to each other through text can come to feel closer, and think better of each other, than people meeting face to face. The writer chooses what to show, the reader fills the gaps with idealized guesses, and each reply confirms the image. That is both a power and a trap. James Pennebaker's research on expressive writing, begun in 1986, shows that putting feelings into words clarifies them, so a lover who writes often discovers what they feel by writing it. The tradition is ancient. Ovid's Heroides imagines letters from heroines, Penelope, Dido, Ariadne, to the men who left them, and makes the letter a theatre of longing. Centuries later Franz Kafka, who conducted most of his loves by post, named the shadow: writing letters, he told Milena Jesenská in 1922, was an intercourse with ghosts, and written kisses never reached their destination but were drunk on the way. Letters let you be more eloquent, more patient and more perceptive than you can be in a crowded room. They also let both people fall in love with the letter itself. The art is to write as yourself, and then to come and stand behind your words.

tales.title: To Her Master, or Rather Father
tales.who: Heloise and Peter Abelard
tales.when: c. 1115 to 1164; the letters c. 1132 to 1135
tales.where: Paris, the abbey of Saint-Denis and the convent of the Paraclete in Champagne
tales.source: Abelard, Historia calamitatum (c. 1132) and the letters of Abelard and Heloise; their authenticity was once questioned, but most scholars now accept them
tales.tale:
Around 1115 Peter Abelard was the most famous teacher in Paris, a thinker who drew students from across Europe and beat his own masters in open debate. Heloise was the niece of Fulbert, a churchman of Notre-Dame, and she was already known for her learning, rare in anyone young and rarer still in a woman. Abelard arranged to lodge in Fulbert's house as her teacher. With their books open before them, he later confessed, more words of love passed between them than words of reading, and more kisses than lessons.

Soon the whole city knew. Love songs Abelard wrote for her were sung in the streets. Heloise bore a son, Astrolabe. Abelard insisted on a secret marriage. Heloise argued against it; she wanted no chain on him. Fulbert, feeling betrayed, sent men who broke into Abelard's room at night and castrated him. Abelard became a monk at Saint-Denis. At his bidding, Heloise became a nun.

For over ten years they lived apart. Then, around 1132, Abelard wrote to an unnamed friend a long account of his troubles: the Historia calamitatum, the Story of My Misfortunes. A copy reached Heloise, by then head of the convent of the Paraclete, a house he had given her. She read her own life there, and took up her pen.

Her letter opens with a greeting that has become famous: to her master, or rather father; to her husband, or rather brother; from his handmaid, or rather daughter; his wife, or rather sister. Then she scolds him. You wrote at length to comfort a friend, she says, and not a word to me, who am bound to you by every tie. She never wanted a husband's shelter or his wealth, she tells him, only him. If Augustus, ruler of the whole world, offered to marry her, she would find it dearer and more honourable to be called Abelard's whore than the emperor's empress. In a later letter she admits that even at prayer her mind goes back to their pleasures.

Abelard answered as a monk, turning her toward God. She wrote again, and again, and slowly the letters became a long talk about love, honesty and the life of faith between two of the finest minds of their age. (The letters were once doubted; most scholars now accept them.)

When Abelard died in 1142, Heloise had his body brought to the Paraclete. In 1164 she was laid beside him. Their letters remain: a love that, shut out of every other door, lived on in words.
tales.reveals: Heloise's letters show that writing can carry a love no other channel can reach: candid, precise, unafraid. She seduces not with flattery but with naked honesty and intelligence, and her words have outlived every face that ever turned heads in Paris.

tales.title: A Thousand Kisses, and No Reply
tales.who: Napoleon Bonaparte and Josephine de Beauharnais
tales.where: Paris and the roads and camps of northern Italy, from Nice to Milan
tales.source: Napoleon's letters to Josephine (1796), published in many editions; Andrew Roberts, Napoleon the Great (2014)
tales.tale:
On 9 March 1796 a thin, burning general of twenty-six married a widow six years older, in a plain civil ceremony in Paris. Two days later Napoleon Bonaparte rode away to take command of the Army of Italy. Josephine stayed behind, in the city she loved.

He wrote to her from the road, from his headquarters, between battles, sometimes more than once a day. The letters are among the most fevered ever written by a man with an army to run. He tells her he has not spent a day without loving her, nor a night without clasping her in his arms. He cannot drink a cup of tea without cursing the glory and ambition that keep him from the soul of his life. He sends a thousand kisses, then a kiss on her heart, and one much lower. He carries her picture everywhere, and when its glass broke one day, an aide later recalled, he took it as a sign of ill luck and went pale.

Her letters were few, short and late. Josephine had married partly to be safe. She found her new husband's fire strange, a little frightening, almost comic. In Paris she was enjoying the charm of a young officer, Hippolyte Charles. Her silences drove Napoleon wild. You do not write to me, he complains, letter after letter. Then he pleads. Then he accuses. Then he forgives. He begs her to come to Italy. She pleads illness, hints that she is with child, and stays.

Meanwhile he was winning: Montenotte, Lodi, Milan. Europe was learning his name. Only in the summer, pressed by the government in Paris, did Josephine make the journey to join him in Milan. And Hippolyte Charles, it came out, travelled with her.

The story has a strange second turn. Napoleon's passion cooled after he learned of her unfaithfulness during the Egyptian campaign of 1798, while hers grew warm. By the time she loved him truly, he held the power. In December 1809, needing an heir, he divorced her, and they parted in tears. When he died on Saint Helena in 1821, those by his bed said her name was among his last words.

The letters of 1796 show a man courting on paper with everything he had: speed, heat, a single fixed thought. They also show what letters cannot do alone. Words poured into silence turn into pleading, and a passion that is never answered becomes a kind of shouting.
tales.reveals: Napoleon's letters prove that words alone can carry enormous heat across distance. But seduction by letter is a conversation, not a broadcast: without listening, rhythm and reply, eloquence curdles into pleading, and the one who writes less ends up holding the power.

practice: Write one real letter by hand this week to a woman you desire or love, naming a specific moment you shared and what you noticed about her in it.
In messages, answer what she actually wrote before adding your own news, and quote back a phrase of hers that stayed with you.
Make one message a day a small gift rather than logistics: an image, a line from what you are reading, a sensory detail of where you are.
Roughly match her rhythm; if your messages keep outnumbering hers three to one, pause, and let the space invite a reply.
principles.shadow: Letters can become a stage for an idealized self, or a flood that demands an answer the other cannot give. Never write what you would not stand behind in person, and never use the written word to pressure, guilt or keep someone on a string.

principles.title: Open, step by step
principles.motto: Intimacy is a staircase: one honest step, then wait for hers.
principles.essence: Closeness is not declared; it is built, one disclosure answered by another. Reveal yourself in layers, match the other's pace, and let each confidence be received before you offer the next. The slow, mutual unveiling is itself the seduction.
principles.depth: Irwin Altman and Dalmas Taylor described relationships in their social penetration theory (1973) as a gradual movement inward, from the broad, shallow layers of the self toward the narrow, deep ones, like peeling an onion. A meta-analysis by Nancy Collins and Lynn Carol Miller (1994) found three linked effects: we like people who disclose to us, we disclose more to people we like, and we come to like those to whom we have disclosed. But depth alone is not intimacy. Harry Reis and Phillip Shaver (1988) argued that intimacy is a process: one person reveals, the other responds with understanding, validation and care, and the first person feels it. Diary studies by Jean-Philippe Laurenceau and colleagues (1998) supported this: feeling met mattered as much as speaking. Timing matters too. Very personal material offered too early tends to unsettle rather than charm, because it skips the reciprocity that makes trust feel earned. The philosopher Martin Buber, in I and Thou (1923), wrote that all real living is meeting: not a monologue delivered at someone, but an encounter in which both are changed. Disclosure seduces because it is a gift that invites one in return.

tales.title: Thirty-Six Questions on Long Island
tales.who: Arthur Aron, Elaine Aron and pairs of student volunteers
tales.where: State University of New York at Stony Brook
tales.source: Aron, Melinat, Aron, Vallone and Bator, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 1997
tales.tale:
The room was plain: two chairs, a table, an envelope of printed slips, and a white light humming in the ceiling over a campus on Long Island. Two students who had never met sat down face to face. They had signed up for a psychology study and expected a form to fill in. Instead the instructions said: take turns, read each slip aloud, both of you answer, and do not rush.

The first slip was easy. 'Given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest?' They laughed and named a singer and a grandmother, and the ice cracked a little. 'What would constitute a perfect day for you?' Another laugh. But now something small slipped out: a lake at dawn, a father who used to wake early to fish.

Fifteen minutes in, the second set began, and the questions leaned closer. 'What is your most treasured memory?' 'If you knew that in one year you would die suddenly, would you change anything about the way you are now living?' The young man paused longer than he meant to. The young woman did not fill the silence. She waited. And he saw that she waited.

The last set asked them to say true things that began with 'we'. We are both in this room feeling... nervous, he offered. Curious, she said. Then: 'When did you last cry in front of another person? By yourself?' And at last, number thirty-six: share a problem of your own, ask the other for advice, and ask them to tell you back how you seem to feel about it.

Forty-five minutes. No lessons in flirting, no matching of opinions. The researchers, Arthur and Elaine Aron and their colleagues, even paired some students who disagreed about things they cared about, and those pairs grew close too. Other pairs spent the same time on small talk ('What is your favorite holiday? Why?'). The question pairs said they felt far closer, in one comparison as close as many students felt in the closest bond of their lives.

The study measured closeness, not love, and the authors said so plainly. Yet the questions travelled far beyond that room, retold in newspapers and essays as a recipe for falling in love, with stories of people from the study who later married. What happened in that room was simple. Each question asked a little more than the one before. Each answer was received, gently, before the next was risked.
tales.reveals: Closeness grew not from one dramatic confession but from escalating, reciprocal, turn-taking disclosure, each step answered before the next. The structure made vulnerability feel safe because it was shared and paced.

tales.title: Will You Marry Me, June?
tales.who: Johnny Cash and June Carter
tales.where: London Gardens arena, London, Ontario, Canada
tales.source: Johnny Cash, Man in Black (1975) and Cash: The Autobiography (1997); Robert Hilburn, Johnny Cash: The Life (2013)
tales.tale:
A full hall in a Canadian February, a woman at a man's shoulder. By the winter of 1968, June Carter had known Johnny Cash for more than ten years, and she had seen nearly all of him. They had met backstage at the Grand Ole Opry in 1956, both married to other people. Since 1961 she had toured with his show and sung beside him, and in 1963, with Merle Kilgore, she had written a song about falling into a burning ring of fire.

She had also seen the other man. That one swallowed pep pills, amphetamines, by the handful. He missed shows and wrecked cars, and in 1965 he was arrested at El Paso with hundreds of pills stuffed into his guitar case. She flushed his pills away. He found more. In 1967, with his parents and a Nashville doctor beside her, she helped him through the hard, shaking weeks of getting clean.

He had asked her to marry him, in private, more than once. She had always said no. She had been through two divorces, and she knew exactly what she would be marrying.

On 22 February, at the London Gardens arena in London, Ontario, the house was full: some five thousand people, by most reports. Partway through the set, Cash stopped the music and turned to her in front of all of them. Will you marry me, June? The stories of what she did first do not agree. Some say she laughed it off and told him to get on with the show. Others say she simply stood there, stunned. The crowd began to call out. He asked again. This time she said yes, and the hall roared.

They married a week later, on 1 March, in Franklin, Kentucky. The marriage lasted thirty-five years, through falls as well as triumphs, until June died in May 2003. Johnny followed her four months later.

What made that night matter was not the show of it. A proposal before thousands can be a trap, a way to make no impossible, and June had every reason to resist one. It worked because nothing was hidden anymore: the cravings, the shame, the slow road back. He was not asking her to love a legend dressed in black. He was asking a woman who had seen him at his worst whether she still wanted to stand beside him. And he asked it, at last, in a place where he could not hide.
tales.reveals: The public proposal was only the final, visible step of years of private disclosure, much of it humiliating. Intimacy that has already survived the truth can afford a grand gesture; intimacy that has not cannot.

practice: This week, answer one ordinary question with a true detail you would usually skip: not your job title, but the lake and the father who fished. Then stop, and let her answer back.
Match, then deepen by one notch: when a woman shares something personal, offer something of similar weight, not heavier, and see whether she takes the next step.
When she discloses, respond before you relate: reflect what you heard and what she seems to feel before telling your own story.
Bring a few of Aron's questions to dinner with someone you are drawn to and take turns; the game frame makes depth feel light.
principles.shadow: Disclosure goes wrong when it is dumped too fast, staged to manufacture false intimacy, or extracted from someone not ready to give it. Never use another's confidences as leverage, and never push past a pause she clearly means.

principles.title: Love that enlarges you
principles.motto: Choose the one beside whom you become more of yourself.
principles.essence: The deepest attraction is to someone who makes your world larger: new ideas, new courage, new versions of yourself. Be that person for another, and seek it in return. Love that only flatters you stays small; love that stretches you keeps its fire.
principles.depth: Arthur and Elaine Aron's self-expansion model (1986) proposes that people are driven to enlarge the self, gaining new perspectives, skills, identities and resources, and that a lover is one of the fastest routes, because in close relationships we come to include the other in the self. In a prospective study (Aron, Paris and Aron, 1995), students tested repeatedly over a semester showed a greater increase in the diversity of their self-descriptions, and in self-efficacy, after falling in love. Later experiments (Aron and colleagues, 2000) had couples complete a novel, mildly challenging task, crawling bound together across gym mats, and found gains in reported relationship quality compared with a dull task; the effect is real but modest. Stephen Drigotas and colleagues (1999) named the Michelangelo phenomenon: partners who see and affirm our ideal self help sculpt us toward it. The thought is ancient. Aristotle, in the Nicomachean Ethics (Books VIII and IX), held that the highest friendship joins people who love each other's goodness and so become better together, each a second self to the other. Rilke, in his Letters to a Young Poet (1904), called love a high inducement for the individual to ripen.

tales.title: Two Dreams and a Leaking Shed
tales.who: Marie Sklodowska Curie and Pierre Curie
tales.source: Marie Curie, Pierre Curie (1923) and her Autobiographical Notes; Pierre Curie's letters of 1894; Eve Curie, Madame Curie (1937)
tales.tale:
A tall man in the deep of a window that opens onto a balcony: that is how Maria Sklodowska remembered Pierre Curie, with a grave and gentle face, and seeming very young. It was 1894. The Polish physicist Józef Kowalski had invited them both to his rooms because he thought one might help the other. She was twenty-six, studying at the Sorbonne on almost nothing, and she needed a laboratory where she could measure how steels behave as magnets. He was thirty-five, taught at the city's School of Industrial Physics and Chemistry, and knew magnetism as well as anyone in France.

He did not court her with flowers. He sent her his paper on symmetry in physics, with a note written inside. When she went home to Warsaw that summer, unsure if she would ever come back to France, he wrote that it would be a beautiful thing, a thing he dared not hope for, to pass their lives near each other, 'hypnotized by our dreams: your patriotic dream, our humanitarian dream, and our scientific dream.' If need be, he offered, he would move to Poland.

She came back. They married on 26 July 1895 at Sceaux, a plain town-hall wedding with no rings. She wore a dark blue dress she could later wear in the laboratory. They spent a wedding gift on two bicycles and rode through the summer lanes of the Île-de-France.

What followed was a marriage lived mostly at a workbench. Pierre set aside his own work on crystals to join her study of the strange rays that came from uranium. In a leaking shed on the rue Lhomond, freezing in winter and stifling in summer, they worked by hand through tonnes of pitchblende waste, a dark rock that holds uranium. In 1898 they announced polonium, named for her divided country, and radium. Some evenings they walked back just to look. Tubes of radium salts glowed on the shelves, she wrote, like faint fairy lights.

In 1903 the Nobel committee seemed set to honour only Pierre and Henri Becquerel. Warned by the mathematician Gösta Mittag-Leffler, Pierre wrote that he wished to be considered together with Madame Curie. She shared the prize.

In April 1906 Pierre was killed by a horse-drawn wagon in the rue Dauphine. Marie took over his chair at the Sorbonne, its first woman professor, and in 1911 won a second Nobel prize alone. The dream he had named in a letter outlived him, carried by the woman he had helped her become.
tales.reveals: Neither Curie shrank to fit the other: each made room, gave up something, and insisted on the other's full stature. Their attraction was not a refuge from ambition but a shared enlargement of it.

tales.title: A Year of Songs
tales.who: Clara Wieck and Robert Schumann
tales.source: The Marriage Diaries of Robert and Clara Schumann, ed. Gerd Nauhaus; Nancy B. Reich, Clara Schumann: The Artist and the Woman (1985)
tales.tale:
A girl of eleven at the piano in her father's house in Leipzig, and a young man with his head in the clouds come to live under the same roof. Clara Wieck was already a wonder child. Her father, Friedrich Wieck, had built her into one, and he meant to keep her. Robert Schumann was a restless law student, his head full of Jean Paul's novels, come to study piano with her father. He told the Wieck children ghost stories. By November 1835, when Clara was sixteen, he had kissed her on the stairs, and she had become the heart of his music.

Wieck fought them for five years. He forbade their letters, dragged Clara off on concert tours, and called Robert a drunkard. The lovers wrote in secret, and in 1839 they took her father to court. The court found for them. On 12 September 1840, the day before Clara turned twenty-one, they married in the village church at Schönefeld, just outside Leipzig.

That year Robert, who had written almost only for piano, poured out well over a hundred songs. As a wedding present he gave Clara the set called Myrthen, named for the myrtle in a bride's wreath. On their first day as husband and wife they began a shared diary, taking turns week by week, writing of music and money, quarrels and books. They studied Bach's fugues together and read Shakespeare aloud.

The diary is honest about the cost. One home held one piano, and when Robert composed, Clara could not practise. She bore eight children. In 1839 she had written that a woman must not wish to compose, since none had ever managed it, so why should she be the one? Yet inside the marriage she wrote her Piano Trio in G minor, and songs that Robert published beside his own. She carried his music to crowds who did not yet understand it, and on New Year's Day 1846, in Leipzig, she gave the first performance of his Piano Concerto.

Then Robert's mind darkened. In February 1854 he threw himself into the Rhine at Düsseldorf. He spent his last two years in a hospital for the mind at Endenich, and died in 1856. Clara was thirty-six, with seven living children. She went back on the road and played for nearly thirty-five more years, editing his works and playing them in city after city, until they belonged to the world.

Each made the other larger, and neither paid evenly.
tales.reveals: Love released a torrent of creation in both Schumanns, and their shared diary shows growth built on talk, study and mutual admiration. It also shows that one partner's expansion can be paid for by the other's narrowed hours, and that growth must be tended on both sides.

practice: Plan one genuinely new thing together this week, a class, an unknown trail, a cuisine neither of you can cook, and notice the energy between you afterwards.
Ask, 'What are you trying to become this year?' Then, over the following days, find one concrete way to help her toward it.
Name a quality you admire in her that she has not fully claimed yet, and say it as plain fact rather than flattery.
Keep a passion of your own that she cannot fully enter; you need something to bring back to the table.
principles.shadow: Growth goes wrong when one partner's expansion is paid for by the other's shrinking, or when you treat a lover as a project to improve. Enlarge, do not remodel: support who she wants to become, not who you want her to be.

principles.title: To be truly known
principles.motto: Be the one who sees the whole of her, and stays.
principles.essence: Beneath the wish to be admired lies a deeper hunger: to be seen accurately, flaws and all, and wanted anyway. Learn to know people as they truly are, say back what you see, and let yourself be known in turn. Nothing binds like recognition.
principles.depth: William Swann's self-verification theory (1983) holds that people want others to see them as they see themselves, because accurate recognition makes the world predictable and the self feel real. In one study (Swann, Hixon and De La Ronde, 1992) married people were more committed to spouses who saw them as they saw themselves, even when those self-views were unflattering, while dating partners cared more about being admired. Yet Sandra Murray, John Holmes and Dale Griffin (1996) found that the happiest couples also hold positive illusions, seeing each other a little more generously than each sees themselves. The findings fit together: we long to be known accurately and held generously, which Harry Reis calls perceived partner responsiveness, the felt sense of being understood, validated and cared for. Philosophy got there first. Hegel, in the Phenomenology of Spirit (1807), argued that self-consciousness becomes itself only through being recognized by another self-consciousness. Montaigne, explaining his friendship with Étienne de La Boétie, could only say: 'Because it was he, because it was I' (Essays I.28). To be recognized is to have your existence confirmed by a witness who chose to look closely.

tales.title: The Other Half
tales.who: Aristophanes, Socrates and the guests of Agathon
tales.when: set in 416 BC; written c. 385 to 370 BC
tales.source: Plato, Symposium 189c to 193d (philosophical dialogue; the myth is Plato's invention, placed in Aristophanes' mouth)
tales.tale:
Lamps burn low in Agathon's house in Athens on the second night of the party. The young playwright Agathon has just won the prize for tragedy at the Lenaia festival, and his guests, still aching from the first night, agree to drink gently and take turns praising Eros, the god of love. When the comic poet Aristophanes' turn comes, he has the hiccups. The doctor Eryximachus, asked to cure him or speak in his place, does both, and prescribes holding the breath, gargling, and if all else fails, a good sneeze.

Then Aristophanes, cured, tells the strangest story of the night. (It is Plato's story, really, set in the poet's mouth. But let him tell it.)

Once, he says, people were not as we are. Each was round, with four arms and four legs and two faces looking opposite ways on one neck. They came in three kinds: the male, born of the sun; the female, born of the earth; and a third kind, male and female at once, born of the moon. They went rolling along fast, like acrobats turning cartwheels on eight limbs, so strong and proud that they tried to climb to heaven and attack the gods.

Zeus did not destroy them, for then he would lose their sacrifices. He cut each one in two, the way you slice sorb-apples (a small hard fruit) for pickling, or an egg with a hair. He told Apollo to turn the faces round and draw the skin together at the belly, tied in a knot we still call the navel, so that we would remember.

After that, each half longed for the other. They clung to each other and would not let go, and began to die of hunger and idleness. So Zeus took pity and changed their bodies so that holding each other could bring rest, and they could go back to the work of living.

And when someone meets their own other half, Aristophanes says, they are struck with friendship and closeness and love, and will hardly be apart for a moment. Yet they cannot say what they want from each other. Suppose Hephaestus, smith of the gods, stood over them and offered to weld them into one, to live and die as one: neither would refuse. Love, he ends, is the name for the desire and pursuit of the whole.

The guests laugh, as they are meant to. Then Socrates speaks and gently disagrees. Love, he says, seeks not our missing half, but the good.
tales.reveals: Aristophanes captures the uncanny feeling of recognition: meeting someone and sensing you have been known before you have explained yourself. Plato lets Socrates complicate it, a reminder that being completed by another is not the same as being made better.

tales.title: Till This Moment I Never Knew Myself
tales.who: Elizabeth Bennet and Fitzwilliam Darcy
tales.source: Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice (1813), a novel
tales.tale:
Candles blaze in the assembly rooms at Meryton, the music starts, and a rich, tall, bored young man will not dance. This is a novel, Jane Austen's, and it begins with an insult. Urged by his friend Bingley to dance with Elizabeth Bennet, Mr Darcy glanced at her and said, loud enough for her to hear, 'She is tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt me.' Elizabeth laughed and told the story to her friends with great spirit. She had, Austen tells us, a lively, playful nature that delighted in anything ridiculous.

Each decided they had seen the other whole. He saw a country girl with a coarse family. She saw pride, and then, once the charming Mr Wickham had told his tale, cruelty.

Yet Darcy kept looking: her fine eyes, her three-mile walk through the mud to nurse her sister, the way she argued with him without wanting anything from him. At the parsonage at Hunsford he proposed, in a speech that was half love and half insult. 'In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed.' He loved her, he made plain, against his will, his reason, even his character. She refused. He was the last man in the world she could ever be persuaded to marry. He had not, she told him, behaved like a gentleman.

Then came the letter. Darcy, stung, wrote through the night and gave her the truth about Wickham, and his own part in parting Bingley from her sister. She read it walking in the lane, again and again, until the ground shifted under her feet. 'How despicably have I acted!' she cried to herself. 'Till this moment I never knew myself.'

That is the hinge of the book. Seeing truly runs both ways, and it costs them both. She had to see her own prejudice before she could see him. He had to take her rebuke to heart before he could change, and at Pemberley, months later, she met a man who had.

Walking together near Longbourn, he asked again, and she said yes. Later she asked what had first drawn him. He could not fix on the hour, or the spot, or the look, or the words: he was 'in the middle before I knew that I had begun.' She found the answer herself, half teasing. He had been sick of politeness and bowing, of women who looked and thought only to please him. She had caught him because she was so unlike them.
tales.reveals: Darcy and Elizabeth fall in love only after each has been accurately, painfully seen, and has seen themselves. Recognition that includes the flaws, and stays, is far more binding than admiration.

practice: Once this week, tell a woman a true observation about her that is neither compliment nor critique, such as 'You go quiet when you are proud of something,' and watch her face.
Ask a follow-up to her follow-up: the third question is usually where people start to feel known.
Let yourself be seen: admit a misjudgment you once made about someone, as Elizabeth did, and notice how it changes the room.
Before you decide who a woman is, give her a second scene; most first impressions are Darcy at the assembly.
principles.shadow: Recognition becomes control when 'I know you' is used to box a woman in, to predict and dismiss her, or to expose what she shared in trust. Seeing her deeply gives you no right to define her; the knowing must stay open and humble.

principles.title: Kindness is magnetic
principles.motto: Be the harbour, and she will keep sailing home to you.
principles.essence: Excitement may light the spark, but people stay where they feel safe: noticed, protected, never mocked for reaching out. Make your kindness reliable and specific, and you become someone desire can rest in rather than fear.
principles.depth: In David Buss's survey of more than ten thousand people across 37 cultures (1989), kindness and understanding ranked at or near the top of the traits desired in a long-term mate, for women and men alike, above good looks and earning power. Attachment theory explains why. John Bowlby described the secure base and safe haven a child needs; Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver (1987) showed that adult romantic love runs on the same system, and Brooke Feeney's later work (2004) found that people whose partners support them securely explore more boldly, not less. Safety need not smother desire, as some fear. Gurit Birnbaum, Harry Reis and colleagues (2016) found that when a partner responded with understanding and care, people reported more sexual desire for them, perhaps because responsiveness signals someone valuable and worth keeping close. The Hebrew Bible has a word for this quality: hesed, loyal loving-kindness that goes beyond what duty requires. Iris Murdoch defined love as the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real (1959). Kindness is that realisation made visible, and people are drawn to it because, at last, they can rest.

tales.title: Handfuls Left on Purpose
tales.who: Ruth, Naomi and Boaz
tales.when: set in the time of the Judges; written perhaps 6th to 4th century BC (dating debated)
tales.source: Book of Ruth, chapters 1 to 4 (Hebrew Bible; quotations from the King James Version)
tales.tale:
Barley stands gold around Bethlehem, and a foreign widow walks behind the reapers. Ruth had nothing to recommend her there. She was a Moabite, from a people the Israelites did not trust, and a widow. When her mother-in-law Naomi, who had lost her husband and both sons, decided to walk home from Moab, she told her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. One did. Ruth would not. 'Whither thou goest, I will go,' she said, 'and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.'

They came as the barley harvest began, so poor that Ruth went out to glean: to gather the stalks the reapers dropped, as the law let the poor and the stranger do. She happened, the story says with a straight face, on the field of Boaz, a rich kinsman of Naomi's late husband.

Boaz noticed her at once. Then he did a string of quiet things. He told her to stay in his field, close to his young women. He told his young men not to touch her. When thirsty, she should drink from the jars his men had filled. At the meal he passed her roasted grain until she had more than enough. And when she rose to work again, he told his reapers to pull handfuls from their bundles and let them fall for her to find, and not to scold her.

Ruth bowed low and asked the question the book turns on: why have I found grace in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, seeing I am a stranger? Because, he said, he had heard what she had done for Naomi.

At the end of the harvest Naomi thought of a bold plan. Ruth washed, put on sweet oil, and went by night to the threshing floor where Boaz slept beside the grain. She uncovered his feet and lay down. Scholars still argue how much the Hebrew of that night implies. At midnight he woke, startled, and found a woman there. 'Spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid,' she said, 'for thou art a near kinsman.' It was a proposal, and she made it.

He did not take advantage of the dark. He blessed her kindness and sent her home before dawn with six measures of barley in her shawl. Next morning he settled the matter, openly and with honour, at the city gate. Their son Obed, the book ends, was grandfather to King David.
tales.reveals: Boaz's attraction lies less in wealth than in the way he protects without possessing, giving in ways that spare Ruth's dignity. His kindness made it safe for her to take the bold step herself.

tales.title: Look at That Bird
tales.who: John Gottman, Janice Driver and newlywed couples
tales.source: Driver and Gottman, Family Process, 2004; Gottman and DeClaire, The Relationship Cure (2001). The couple below is an illustrative composite.
tales.tale:
Sun through a wide window falls on a sofa, a small kitchen, a pile of newspapers and a bag of groceries. It looked like a pleasant bed-and-breakfast. It was also a laboratory. At the University of Washington, the psychologist John Gottman and his colleagues invited newlywed couples to spend a day there, living as they usually would, while cameras on the walls recorded them and sensors at times tracked their heartbeats. The newspapers called it the Love Lab.

Picture one such couple. They are not real people but a composite, drawn from the published work. It is Sunday morning. He stands at the window with his coffee. She is reading. 'Look at that,' he says, nodding outside. 'There's a goldfinch on the railing.'

It is nothing. It is not about the bird. Gottman called a moment like this a bid: a small reach for attention, interest, humour or comfort. And he saw that partners answered bids in three ways. They could turn toward: she looks up, comes to the window, says, 'Oh, look at the yellow on it.' They could turn away: she keeps reading, or murmurs without lifting her head. Or they could turn against: 'Can't you see I'm reading?'

The researchers who watched these tapes, Janice Driver among them, marked down thousands of such moments. Most were tiny: a word about the weather, a sigh, a joke, a hand on a shoulder in passing. Each carried a hidden question. Are you there for me? Do I matter enough to make you look up from your page?

Years later the lab followed the couples up. In Gottman's account, those still together six years on had turned toward each other's bids about eighty-six per cent of the time in the apartment. Those who had divorced had done so about a third of the time. Driver and Gottman also found that couples who turned toward each other in ordinary moments brought more humour and warmth into their later fights. The small kindnesses were savings they could draw on when times were hard.

The larger claims need care. Gottman's claims to predict divorce almost for certain have drawn serious criticism, since his models were fitted after the outcomes were already known. But the finding about bids has the plainness of something true. Love was not decided by grand gestures. It was decided at the window, over a bird, again and again: whether one person reached, and whether the other reached back.
tales.reveals: Safety is built from hundreds of small responses, not from declarations. Each time you turn toward a bid, you teach someone that reaching for you is safe, and that is what keeps desire alive.

practice: Count bids this week: notice each small reach, a remark, a sigh, a 'look at this', and turn toward it with real attention, even for ten seconds.
Do one kindness without announcing it, your own version of Boaz's dropped handfuls: something that makes her day easier and asks for no thanks.
When a woman shows you something tender or embarrassing, never make it material for a joke later; let her learn that what she gives you is safe.
On a date, make the logistics gentle: clear plans, an easy way home, an easy way to say no. Ease is attractive.
principles.shadow: Kindness curdles when it becomes a strategy to create debt, or when safety means never risking honesty or desire. Be kind, not merely nice: protect without smothering, and never use gentleness to buy what must be freely given.

principles.title: Chosen again and again
principles.motto: Love is a vow renewed each morning, not a feeling kept in a drawer.
principles.essence: Devotion is not the absence of other options; it is choosing the same person again with your eyes open. Let your constancy be active and intelligent, a daily act of will and wit, and it becomes the most seductive thing you can offer: proof that someone will stay.
principles.depth: Caryl Rusbult's investment model (1980, 1983) shows that commitment rests on three supports: satisfaction, the investments you have made, and how attractive the alternatives look. Committed people even rate attractive outsiders as less appealing, a protective bias documented by Dennis Johnson and Rusbult (1989). Robert Sternberg's triangular theory (1986) treats commitment as the decision component of love, distinct from passion and intimacy, and the one most under our control. Does devotion kill passion? Not necessarily. Bianca Acevedo, Arthur Aron, Helen Fisher and Lucy Brown (2012) scanned people married about twenty-one years who said they were still intensely in love; their partner's face activated dopamine-rich reward regions much as in new lovers, along with areas linked to attachment, without the obsessive anxiety of early love. A US survey by K. Daniel O'Leary and colleagues (2012) found roughly forty per cent of people married more than a decade reporting being very intensely in love, though self-report has limits. Erich Fromm wrote in The Art of Loving (1956) that love is not only a strong feeling but a decision, a judgment and a promise. Kierkegaard's Judge William, in Either/Or (1843), argued that married love must be won anew each day.

tales.title: The Shroud Unwoven by Night
tales.who: Penelope and Odysseus
tales.when: myth; the Odyssey was composed c. 8th to 7th century BC
tales.source: Homer, Odyssey, Books 2, 19, 23 and 24
tales.tale:
By torchlight a woman sits at a great loom, pulling out, thread by thread, the work of her own day. Her husband Odysseus had been gone nearly twenty years: ten at Troy, then wanderings no one in Ithaca could follow. More than a hundred young men from the islands had settled into his house to court his wife. They ate his cattle, drank his wine, bedded his maidservants, and pressed Penelope day after day to choose one of them.

She could not simply refuse. She had no husband to stand behind and a young son to protect. So she set up the loom in the hall and told them she would choose once she had finished a burial cloth for her old father-in-law, Laertes, so that no woman could blame her for burying a great man without one. By day she wove. By night she undid it. For three years the suitors waited on a cloth that never grew. In the fourth a maid betrayed her, and they caught her at it.

When Odysseus at last came home dressed as a beggar, Penelope sat with the stranger by the fire late into the night. She told him a dream. She announced a contest with her husband's great bow. Homer leaves it unclear how much she guessed.

The bow was strung, the suitors were killed, and still Penelope did not run into her husband's arms. Their son called her hard-hearted. She sat across the firelight from him and said that if he were truly Odysseus, they would know each other by signs hidden from everyone else. Then she set a trap. She told the old nurse to move their bed out of the bedroom for him.

Odysseus exploded. No one could move that bed. He had built it himself around the trunk of an olive tree growing inside the room, and made the living tree its post. Who had cut it?

Her knees went weak. She ran to him, threw her arms around his neck, and begged him not to be angry that she had not welcomed him at once. She had always feared some man would come and fool her. That night Athena held back the dawn at the edge of the ocean so that the night would last. They went gladly to their old bed, then lay awake telling each other everything.

Homer's world was not fair. Odysseus had lain with goddesses on his way home, and no one asked him to weave.
tales.reveals: Penelope's devotion is not passive waiting but daily, inventive resistance, and her final test proves that faithfulness and sharp judgment belong together. The secret of the rooted bed is what they choose, again, to share.

tales.title: Savitri Follows Death
tales.who: Savitri, Satyavan and Yama, lord of death
tales.when: myth; the Mahabharata was composed c. 400 BC to AD 400
tales.source: Mahabharata, Book of the Forest (Vana Parva), the tale told by the sage Markandeya to Yudhishthira
tales.tale:
Savitri shone so bright, the epic says, that no prince dared to ask for her hand. So her father, King Ashvapati of Madra, told her to go out and choose a husband for herself. She travelled through royal cities and forest retreats and came home having chosen: Satyavan, son of Dyumatsena, a king who had gone blind, lost his kingdom, and now lived in exile in the forest, where his son cut wood and tended the holy fires.

The wise man Narada, visiting the court, turned grave. Satyavan was everything good, he said: generous, truthful, handsome, gentle. But he had one flaw that outweighed all the rest. In a year from that day he would die. Her father begged her to choose again. Savitri answered that some things happen only once: a lot is cast once, a daughter is given once, the words 'I give' are said once. She had chosen in her heart, and she would not choose twice.

So they married. She laid aside her jewels for bark and ochre cloth, served her blind parents-in-law, and counted the days. Three days before the last one she began a vow, fasting and standing day and night. On the morning itself she asked to go with Satyavan into the forest. He was splitting wood when pain went through his head. He lay down with his head in her lap.

Then she saw him: a figure in red, dark and shining, with a noose in his hand. Yama, lord of the dead, drew out of Satyavan a soul no bigger than a thumb, bound it, and set off toward the south. Savitri followed.

Yama told her to go back. She kept walking, and she kept talking. She spoke of dharma, the right way to live, and of friendship: the wise say that walking seven steps together makes people friends, and by that measure she and Death were friends already.
